docs.title: The Project Management Knowledge Atlas
docs.text:
The Project Management Knowledge Atlas is a connected PMP study and project-management reference. It explains how processes, artifacts, decisions, authority, and information flows work together instead of presenting them as isolated definitions.

It is an independent learning resource, not official PMI material or a substitute for current PMI standards, examination guidance, or organizational governance.

Current status

docs.title: Active review stage
docs.text: The Atlas is being reviewed for coverage, source traceability, cross-page consistency, and editorial quality. Treat it as a structured study aid under active review, and verify consequential claims against current PMI and organizational sources.

docs.title: Five complementary viewsProject Lifecycle GuideMaster Project SequenceProcess ReferenceArtifact ReferenceDecision Guides
docs.text:
Begin with the project story

Explains how work unfolds from need and authorization through planning, execution, monitoring, acceptance, transition, closure, and benefits handoff.

Follow the integrated flow

Shows the end-to-end flow of processes, artifacts, handoffs, decisions, and the major transformations from business need to value.

Study process mechanics

Provides detailed pages for the 49 named processes, with their purpose, position, relationships, and practical context.

Understand project records

Explains documents, registers, baselines, records, examples, and downloadable templates used to preserve project information and decisions.

Reason from a situation

Connects scenario and exam-style questions to authority, artifacts, applicable processes, likely next action, and escalation.

docs.title: How to use the Atlas
docs.text:
1. Start with the Project Lifecycle Guide for the overall story.
  2. Use the Master Project Sequence to see the integrated flow.
  3. Open Process Reference pages for process-level mechanics.
  4. Use the Artifact Reference when you need to understand or create a project artifact.
  5. Use Decision Guides for scenario and exam-style reasoning.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: These principles exist to ensure the Atlas reads as though it were written by a single author.

docs.title: Principle 1 — Explain Before Naming
docs.text:
Introduce the concept before introducing PMI terminology.

Readers should understand the idea before memorizing the vocabulary.

docs.title: Principle 2 — Explain Why Before How
docs.text:
Every process exists to solve a project problem.

Explain the problem first.

Then explain the mechanics.

docs.title: Principle 3 — Relationships Matter More Than Lists
docs.text:
Do not present processes or artifacts in isolation.

Always explain:

  • what created it
  • what depends on it
  • what it influences next

docs.title: Principle 4 — Write for Understanding
docs.text:
The goal is not memorization.

The goal is comprehension.

If readers understand the relationships, recall becomes easier.

docs.title: Principle 5 — Use Plain Technical Language
docs.text:
Write clearly and precisely.

Avoid unnecessary rhetorical flourish.

Avoid unnecessary metaphors.

Avoid repetitive stylistic constructions.

Use emphasis sparingly.

docs.title: Principle 6 — One Idea Per Section
docs.text:
Each section should answer one primary question.

Avoid mixing multiple concepts into the same discussion.

docs.title: Principle 7 — Diagrams Replace Paragraphs
docs.text: When a relationship can be shown more clearly with a simple diagram than several paragraphs of text, use a diagram.

docs.title: Principle 8 — Respect PMI Terminology
docs.text:
Use official PMI terminology when referring to processes and artifacts.

Explanatory text may use simpler language, but should never invent competing terminology.

docs.title: Principle 9 — Distinguish Facts from Commentary
docs.text:
Clearly separate:

  • PMI guidance
  • Atlas explanation
  • Practical advice
  • Exam tips

Readers should always know which perspective they are reading.

docs.title: Principle 10 — Write Beyond the Exam
docs.text:
Every chapter should remain useful after certification.

Readers should be able to use the Atlas while managing real projects.

docs.title: Closing Statement
docs.text:
The Atlas is intended to explain project management as an interconnected system of decisions, information, processes, and artifacts.

Every chapter should help readers understand not only what project managers do, but why each activity exists and how it supports the project as a whole.

This document records architecture decisions that shape the editorial and structural direction of the Atlas.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: The Atlas explains project management through relationships between processes, artifacts, decisions, and information rather than presenting isolated definitions.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Readers understand projects more easily when they see how information flows from one process to another.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: Every chapter should explain what a process creates, what depends on it, and why it exists.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
• Presenting isolated definitions for each concept.
  • Structuring the book strictly by PMI chapter taxonomy.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Each process introduces its purpose before discussing mechanics.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Understanding purpose improves retention and helps readers answer situational questions.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: Every process page begins with Purpose and Why This Process Exists.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
• Starting with procedural steps before purpose.
  • Presenting mechanics only.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Narrative sections present processes in logical dependency order rather than strictly following PMBOK chapter organization.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: The PMBOK is a reference standard; the Atlas is a learning and navigation aid.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: The Atlas may present processes in an order that differs from PMBOK while preserving PMI terminology and technical accuracy.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
• Following PMBOK chapter order exactly.
  • Organizing content purely by memorization categories.

docs.title: Decision: Maintain a Neutral Technical Voice
Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: The Atlas uses clear technical prose and avoids unnecessary rhetorical flourishes.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Readers should focus on concepts rather than writing style.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: Prefer concise explanations, numbered lists, and diagrams. Avoid repeated stylistic constructions and unnecessary metaphors.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
• Using a more narrative or literary tone.
  • Adding frequent rhetorical devices for emphasis.

docs.title: Decision: Separate Authorship from Repository Maintenance
Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Substantive project management content is authored collaboratively and then integrated into the repository.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Separating conceptual authorship from repository maintenance improves consistency and auditability.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: Repository automation should not independently author major content.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
• Generating content automatically from templates alone.
  • Mixing editorial drafting and repository maintenance in one workflow.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: The Atlas uses separate diagram types for sequence, dependency, and lifecycle.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Each diagram should communicate one kind of relationship clearly.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: Avoid diagrams that attempt to explain multiple concepts simultaneously.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
• Using a single composite diagram for everything.
  • Combining sequence and dependency into one visual model.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Major sections should begin by answering a practical project management question whenever appropriate.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Readers naturally approach project management through problems rather than taxonomy.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Examples:

  • Why is the Project Charter needed before planning begins?
  • Why is the Requirements Traceability Matrix created before defining scope?

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
• Starting sections with definitions.
  • Starting sections with taxonomy lists only.

docs.title: Decision: Separate Lifecycle Narrative from Process Mechanics
Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: The Project Lifecycle Guide owns cross-process sequence, concurrent work, handoffs, feedback, and changing project conditions. Process pages retain process purpose, mechanics, authority, and direct relationships; artifact pages retain artifact structure and states; Decision Guides retain scenario choices.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: The Confluence source contains a useful end-to-end narrative but repeats process and artifact detail. Explicit ownership preserves the relational value without creating a second Process Reference.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: Lifecycle order, phase emphasis, links, deferrals, shared terminology, and provenance are registered in definitions/lifecycle.yaml. Generated lifecycle regions and navigation must remain current. Lifecycle prose summarizes and links rather than reproducing full ITTO catalogs.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
• Copying each Confluence chapter into a public page.
  • Expanding the Master Project Sequence until it also served as the detailed lifecycle guide.
  • Maintaining process and artifact links independently in every chapter.

docs.title: Decision: Preserve the Closure and Benefits Boundary as Source-Limited
Status
docs.text: Accepted pending source resolution

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: The Atlas distinguishes formal project closure from continuing benefits ownership and requires an explicit handoff. It does not assert that all benefits must be realized before closure or that closure ends benefits responsibility.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: The Confluence snapshot places benefits measurement after formal closure, while the former Master Project Sequence wording defined project completion through realized value. The registered primary-source material does not resolve that boundary.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: The unsupported absolute statement was removed. Post-project benefits authority, measurement, and sustainment remain deferred until current PMI or framework sources are registered and reviewed.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
• Treating the Confluence wording as authoritative PMI guidance.
  • Retaining the former absolute completion statement.
  • Omitting benefits ownership from transition and closure entirely.

docs.title: Editorial rules
docs.text:
• Explain concepts before terminology.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: DRAFT — Pending Editorial Review

docs.title: Why Projects Exist
docs.text:
Projects exist because organizations need to move from an observed need to a durable result. The transformation framework in this section helps readers see that project work is not a collection of isolated activities. It is a sequence of changes in state, each one answering a different project question and creating new conditions for the next stage.

This framework is a conceptual map. It is not a new PMI methodology. It is a way to organize the Atlas around the major transitions that occur as a project moves from a business need to realized value.

docs.title: The Six Project Transformations
docs.text:
The six transformations describe how a project evolves from an initial opportunity or problem to an outcome that creates value. They also show why artifacts matter. Each transformation produces or updates artifacts that make the next stage possible, and each transformation creates a new level of clarity, commitment, or accountability.

The framework is useful because it helps readers connect sequence, artifacts, and decisions. It also clarifies that project work is often iterative and concurrent rather than strictly linear. A project may plan, execute, and adjust in parallel as uncertainty is reduced and new information appears.

docs.title: Planning Process Group Reference Order
docs.text:
The Atlas uses the following canonical order to reference and navigate the 24 processes in the Planning Process Group. This ordering gives each process a stable position; it does not claim that planning must occur once in a rigid chronology. Planning processes overlap, iterate, and may be revisited as project information changes.

Position Process Knowledge area 01 Develop Project Management Plan Integration 02 Plan Scope Management Scope 03 Collect Requirements Scope 04 Define Scope Scope 05 Create WBS Scope 06 Plan Schedule Management Schedule 07 Define Activities Schedule 08 Sequence Activities Schedule 09 Estimate Activity Durations Schedule 10 Develop Schedule Schedule 11 Plan Cost Management Cost 12 Estimate Costs Cost 13 Determine Budget Cost 14 Plan Quality Management Quality 15 Plan Resource Management Resource 16 Estimate Activity Resources Resource 17 Plan Communications Management Communications 18 Plan Risk Management Risk 19 Identify Risks Risk 20 Perform Qualitative Risk Analysis Risk 21 Perform Quantitative Risk Analysis Risk 22 Plan Risk Responses Risk 23 Plan Procurement Management Procurement 24 Plan Stakeholder Engagement Stakeholder

docs.title: Planning Quality Before Work Begins
docs.text:
Quality planning is part of the project sequence because a project needs agreed standards before it can manage execution consistently. This section is positioned after requirements and scope information have emerged, because meaningful quality planning depends on knowing what the project is intended to achieve.

The process answers a practical question: what standards will define acceptable work, and how will the team measure them? In the Atlas sequence, this activity supports later quality management and inspection work by establishing the criteria that will be used during execution and review.

The transformation is not a separate method from the rest of the project. It is part of the broader movement from stated need to deliverable reality. Once the project has defined the quality expectations, later work can proceed with clearer measures for evaluation, verification, and acceptance.

For the complete process reference, see Plan Quality Management. Related artifacts include Quality Management Plan, Quality Metrics, Quality-Control Measurements, Verified Deliverables, and Accepted Deliverables. A dependency view is available in the Plan Quality Management dependency map, and a decision guide for inspection failures is available in A Deliverable Fails Quality Inspection.

docs.title: Transformation 1 — Business Need → Business Decision
docs.text:
A project begins with a business need, problem, or opportunity. The first transformation asks whether the organization should act on that need and commit resources to a project response.

The starting condition is an identified need. The resulting condition is a business decision to proceed, defer, or stop. The problem being solved is whether the opportunity is worth pursuing under current constraints. The principal decisions concern priority, feasibility, strategic fit, and expected value.

The primary artifacts involved are the business case, the initial project charter, and related strategic documentation. This transformation enables the next stage by creating the authority to move from intention to formal project initiation.

docs.title: Transformation 2 — Business Decision → Authorized Project
docs.text:
Once a decision has been made to proceed, the organization must establish the project as an authorized effort. This transformation turns a decided direction into an organizational commitment.

The starting condition is a business decision to proceed. The resulting condition is an authorized project with defined sponsor support and an initial mandate. The problem being solved is whether the effort is formally recognized as a project that can be governed. The principal decisions involve sponsor approval, high-level scope boundaries, and initial expectations for delivery.

The primary artifacts involved are the project charter, governance arrangements, and any initial stakeholder alignment materials. This transformation enables planning by giving the project a recognized starting point and a basis for formal coordination.

docs.title: Transformation 3 — Authorized Project → Planned Project
docs.text:
The third transformation turns an authorized project into a planned project. Planning does not mean every uncertainty has been eliminated. It means the project has enough structure to guide work, make tradeoffs, and manage risk.

The starting condition is an authorized project. The resulting condition is a planned project with defined scope, schedule, cost, quality expectations, and approach. The problem being solved is how the work will be carried out and how success will be measured. The principal decisions involve scope definition, approach selection, resource allocation, and risk posture.

The primary artifacts involved include the project management plan, scope statements, schedule information, and other planning outputs that define how the work will proceed. This transformation enables execution by converting intent into an actionable course of action.

docs.title: Transformation 4 — Planned Project → Executed Project
docs.text:
Execution brings the plan into practice. This transformation answers whether the project team can deliver the planned outcomes under real conditions.

The starting condition is a planned project. The resulting condition is an executed project with work being completed, monitored, and adapted. The problem being solved is how to deliver value while managing change, uncertainty, and performance concerns. The principal decisions involve prioritization, issue resolution, change handling, and coordination across workstreams.

The primary artifacts involved include work performance information, change records, status reporting, and updated planning artifacts. This transformation enables the next stage by producing evidence of progress and a basis for acceptance.

docs.title: Transformation 5 — Executed Project → Accepted Solution
docs.text:
The fifth transformation moves the project from delivery activity to formal acceptance. This is the point at which the project team and the requesting organization determine whether the solution is acceptable.

The starting condition is an executed project. The resulting condition is an accepted solution, where deliverables have been reviewed and the customer or sponsor accepts the outcome. The problem being solved is whether the work completed meets the intended need in a way that is acceptable to the receiving organization. The principal decisions involve validation, acceptance criteria, transition readiness, and formal closure of delivery obligations.

The primary artifacts involved include acceptance criteria, validation records, transition materials, and formal acceptance documentation. This transformation enables value realization by creating the conditions for the solution to be used rather than merely delivered.

docs.title: Transformation 6 — Accepted Solution → Business Value
docs.text:
The final transformation connects the accepted solution to business value. The Atlas currently treats formal project closure and continuing benefits ownership as distinct concepts, but the registered source set does not yet resolve exactly when benefits realization should define project completion.

The starting condition is an accepted solution. The resulting condition is realized business value. The problem being solved is whether the accepted outcome produces the intended benefit. The principal decisions involve adoption, measurement, operational integration, and ongoing accountability for results.

The primary artifacts involved include benefits tracking information, operational handoff materials, and performance measures that connect delivery to realized outcomes. The project must make continuing ownership explicit at transition; detailed post-project authority remains deferred pending source verification. See Verification, Acceptance, Transition, and Closure.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The six transformations provide a conceptual map for understanding how projects move from need to value. They help readers see that project work is an interconnected sequence of decisions, artifacts, and transitions. The Atlas uses this structure to explain why each stage exists, what it produces, and what follows next.

flowchart LR
    A[Business Need] --> B[Business Decision]
    B --> C[Authorized Project]
    C --> D[Planned Project]
    D --> E[Executed Project]
    E --> F[Accepted Solution]
    F --> G[Business Value]

docs.title: Reusable Resources
docs.text:
Every published artifact page includes an editable blank template and a filled Atlas example. Narrative and approval artifacts use DOCX; registers, logs, matrices, measures, estimates, and schedules use interoperable CSV. The examples share the fictional ServiceBridge Modernization context so requirement, risk, issue, change, deliverable, acceptance, transition, closure, and benefit records can be followed across pages.

Some artifacts use one common example because their decision purpose and structure do not materially change across delivery approaches. Their pages still explain differences in timing, ownership, granularity, formality, approval, storage, and update cadence.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Accepted Deliverables are deliverables that have passed the formal acceptance process in Validate Scope.

docs.title: Why It Exists
docs.text: The artifact exists because customer or sponsor acceptance is a separate decision from technical verification. A deliverable may be verified as meeting quality criteria but still require formal acceptance before it is considered accepted by the receiving organization.

docs.text: • Validate Scope

docs.title: Updated By

  • Benefits realization and operational handoff

docs.title: Contains
docs.text:
• Deliverables accepted by the customer or sponsor
  • Acceptance criteria and the evidence reviewed
  • The accepting customer, sponsor, product owner, or other designated authority
  • The decision date, conditions, exceptions, and signature or equivalent authorization
  • Associated acceptance decisions and unresolved obligations

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text: Accepted Deliverables are created after Verified Deliverables are reviewed through Validate Scope and accepted by the appropriate authority.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
Accepted Deliverables result from Validate Scope. They are distinct from Verified Deliverables, which are created earlier through Control Quality.

A separate Formal Acceptance Record was evaluated and consolidated here. Acceptance evidence is part of the accepted state and should not be split into a parallel record that can drift from the deliverable decision.

docs.title: Common Exam Confusions
docs.text:
• Assuming verified and accepted are the same condition.
  • Treating acceptance as a purely technical decision rather than a formal project decision.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text: A client signs off on the completed deliverable after reviewing the verified results and confirming that the scope expectations have been met.

docs.title: Practical example and reusable resources
docs.text: The examples use the fictional ServiceBridge Modernization project so related artifacts share dates, budget, requirements, risks, issues, changes, deliverables, acceptance, transition, and benefits context.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Common across approaches. The accepted deliverables keeps the same decision purpose; formality, storage, ownership, and update cadence are tailored to the work.

The filled example uses one shared structure. The comparison below explains how timing, ownership, detail, and cadence may still vary.

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text: Approach Typical timing and detail Ownership and approval Update cadence Predictive / Waterfall Planned earlier and detailed to the level needed for the approved end-to-end commitment. Central approval is common when a baseline, contract, or gate is affected. At control dates, reporting periods, and approved changes. Adaptive / Agile Refined near the work and release horizon; planning and documentation still occur. Teams and product roles decide within delegated boundaries; specialist and governance authority remains. Continuously, per iteration, or per release according to need. Hybrid Fixed obligations are detailed early while solution detail is progressively elaborated. Distributed delivery decisions connect to centralized decisions for baselines, contracts, compliance, and acceptance. Iteration-level updates plus integrated governance reviews.

docs.text: Projects learn and encounter variance. A controlled request preserves the reason, impacts, options, authority, and final disposition instead of allowing informal changes to bypass governance.

docs.title: Created By
docs.text: Executing and monitoring processes may identify a need for change, including Monitor and Control Project Work.

docs.title: Updated By
docs.text: • Perform Integrated Change Control records disposition through the associated control records

docs.title: Used By
docs.text:
• The authorized change-control body or role
  • Direct and Manage Project Work after approval

docs.title: Archived By
docs.text: • Close Project or Phase

docs.title: Contains
docs.text:
1. Requested change, reason, requester, and date.
  2. Affected scope, schedule, cost, quality, risk, resources, contracts, and stakeholders.
  3. Options, recommendation, authority, decision, and implementation status.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text: A need is documented, impacts are analyzed, authorized decision makers approve, reject, or defer it, and approved work is implemented and verified. Rejected requests do not alter controlled baselines.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: A Change Request is a proposal. An Approved Change Request is an authorized state used for implementation.

docs.title: Common Exam Confusions
docs.text:
• Implementing before authorization.
  • Assuming every corrective action changes a baseline.
  • Treating issue logging and change approval as the same act.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text: A security requirement discovered during testing triggers a request that records design, schedule, cost, compliance, and release impacts before the governing body decides.

docs.title: Practical example and reusable resources
docs.text: The examples use the fictional ServiceBridge Modernization project so related artifacts share dates, budget, requirements, risks, issues, changes, deliverables, acceptance, transition, and benefits context.

Hybrid The change requests connects baselined infrastructure and procurement commitments with incrementally refined software delivery.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: The Cost Baseline establishes the approved budget distributed over time for measuring project cost performance.

docs.title: Why It Exists
docs.text: Actual spending has little decision value without an authorized comparison point tied to planned work and timing.

docs.title: Updated By

docs.title: Archived By

docs.title: Contains
docs.text: The authorized, time-phased budget and the approved component values needed for performance comparison.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text: Estimates are aggregated and reconciled with funding constraints. Approval establishes the baseline; actual and forecast information are compared with it; authorized changes create controlled revisions.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: Cost Estimates support budget development. Cost forecasts describe expected outcomes. Neither automatically revises the Cost Baseline.

docs.title: Common Exam Confusions
docs.text:
• Confusing total funding with the performance baseline.
  • Rebaselining to erase an unfavorable variance.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text: A forecast shows that specialist costs will exceed plan. The variance is reported and a change request is evaluated before any baseline revision.

docs.title: Purpose

docs.text: Without explicit authorization, planning and delivery can begin without a recognized mandate, sponsor commitment, or agreed high-level boundary.

docs.title: Updated By

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: The Project Management Plan provides the integrated, approved basis for executing, monitoring, controlling, and closing the project.

docs.title: Why It Exists
docs.text: Scope, schedule, cost, quality, resource, communication, risk, procurement, and stakeholder decisions affect one another. The integrated plan exposes conflicts and establishes how those decisions will be governed together.

docs.title: Archived By

docs.title: Contains
docs.text:

  2. Approved baselines.
  3. Lifecycle, development, review, change, and configuration approaches.
  4. Tailoring decisions and management thresholds.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text: The plan is progressively assembled during planning, approved as an integrated governing record, used during delivery and control, and updated only through the applicable control mechanism.

docs.title: Relationships

  • Updating a baseline merely because actual performance differs.
  • Confusing working project documents with controlled plan components.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text: Before release work begins, the team reconciles the scope, schedule, cost, quality, risk, communication, and procurement approaches. Sponsor-approved thresholds define which variances require escalation.

docs.title: Why It Exists
docs.text: The artifact exists so the project team and stakeholders share a consistent understanding of how quality will be planned, assessed, and maintained throughout the project.

docs.title: Created By
docs.text: • Plan Quality Management

docs.title: Updated By

  • Validate Scope

docs.title: Used By
docs.text:
• Manage Quality
  • Control Quality
  • Validate Scope
  • Project team members responsible for execution and review

docs.title: Archived By
docs.text: • Project archive or knowledge management process

docs.title: Contains
docs.text:
• Quality approach and objectives
  • Roles and responsibilities for quality activities
  • Review and testing methods
  • Acceptance criteria references
  • Quality reporting expectations

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text: The Quality Management Plan is created during planning, used throughout execution and review, and updated when quality expectations or project conditions change.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: The Quality Management Plan is created by Plan Quality Management. It guides Manage Quality and Control Quality, and it provides a basis for acceptance-related activity in Validate Scope.

docs.title: Common Exam Confusions
docs.text:
• Confusing the Quality Management Plan with the quality metrics.
  • Assuming the plan is only a document for audits rather than an operating guide for project work.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text: A construction project uses a quality management plan to define inspection checkpoints, reporting thresholds, and the review sequence for structural and safety requirements.

docs.title: Practical example and reusable resources
docs.text: The examples use the fictional ServiceBridge Modernization project so related artifacts share dates, budget, requirements, risks, issues, changes, deliverables, acceptance, transition, and benefits context.

docs.title: Example
docs.text: Approach Atlas example focus Predictive / Waterfall The quality management plan supports an approved end-to-end plan, stage-gate review, and formal control of affected commitments. Adaptive / Agile The quality management plan is maintained close to the work, refined from feedback, and reviewed at iteration or release cadence without removing governance. Hybrid The quality management plan connects baselined infrastructure and procurement commitments with incrementally refined software delivery.

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text: Approach Typical timing and detail Ownership and approval Update cadence Predictive / Waterfall Planned earlier and detailed to the level needed for the approved end-to-end commitment. Central approval is common when a baseline, contract, or gate is affected. At control dates, reporting periods, and approved changes. Adaptive / Agile Refined near the work and release horizon; planning and documentation still occur. Teams and product roles decide within delegated boundaries; specialist and governance authority remains. Continuously, per iteration, or per release according to need. Hybrid Fixed obligations are detailed early while solution detail is progressively elaborated. Distributed delivery decisions connect to centralized decisions for baselines, contracts, compliance, and acceptance. Iteration-level updates plus integrated governance reviews.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Quality Metrics define the specific measurements that will be used to judge whether work meets the agreed quality expectations.

docs.title: Why It Exists
docs.text: The artifact exists because quality standards are easier to apply when they are expressed as measurable values rather than broad intentions.

  • Unit of measure

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text: Quality Metrics are defined during planning, used during execution and inspection, and may be refined if requirements or conditions change.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: Quality Metrics are created by Plan Quality Management. They are applied by Control Quality and used to support acceptance discussions in Validate Scope.

docs.title: Common Exam Confusions
docs.text:
• Confusing quality metrics with quality-control measurements.
  • Treating a single metric as a complete quality plan.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text: A manufacturing team defines a metric stating that the surface finish must remain within 0.2 millimeters of the target value for all approved units.

Communicates quality findings, trends, defects, audit results, recommendations, and decisions needed.

Quality evidence must be synthesized into findings and decisions rather than left as disconnected measurements.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Requirements Documentation makes stakeholder needs explicit enough to analyze, prioritize, trace, design, verify, and validate.

docs.title: Why It Exists
docs.text: Unrecorded expectations cannot be reliably converted into scope or acceptance evidence. The artifact preserves what is needed while related records preserve why, from whom, and how it will be tested.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text: Needs become documented requirements, are linked through the Requirements Traceability Matrix, inform scope and quality decisions, and remain controlled as delivery evidence accumulates.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: The Requirements Traceability Matrix preserves the chain from a stated need to the work and evidence intended to satisfy it.

docs.title: Why It Exists
docs.text: Traceability reveals orphan requirements, untested scope, unauthorized additions, and deliverables that lack a clear business reason.

docs.text: • Collect Requirements

  • Validate Scope
  • Control Scope

docs.title: Contains
docs.text:
1. Stable requirement identifier and source.
  2. Business objective or intended outcome.
  3. Scope or delivery component.
  4. Verification method, acceptance condition, evidence, and status.
  5. Change history where applicable.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text: The matrix begins with elicited requirements and gains links as scope, delivery, verification, and acceptance progress. It is a living control record, not merely a planning table.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: The matrix references Requirements Documentation; it does not replace the detailed requirement statement or the acceptance record.

  • Treating test completion as formal stakeholder acceptance.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: The Risk Register maintains the working record of identified project risks and their treatment over time.

docs.title: Why It Exists
docs.text: Risk work is iterative. A shared register preserves ownership, analysis, response decisions, triggers, current status, and the history needed for monitoring.

docs.title: Created By
docs.text: • Identify Risks

docs.title: Updated By
docs.text:
• Perform Qualitative Risk Analysis
  • Perform Quantitative Risk Analysis when warranted
  • Plan Risk Responses
  • Implement Risk Responses
  • Monitor Risks

docs.title: Used By
docs.text: Planning, execution, monitoring, change, procurement, quality, stakeholder, and closure work use relevant risk information.

docs.title: Archived By
docs.text: • Close Project or Phase

docs.title: Contains
docs.text:
1. Risk statement, cause, event, and potential effect.
  2. Owner, category, probability, impact, priority, and status.
  3. Response, response owner, trigger, contingency, and residual information where established.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text: Risks are identified, analyzed, assigned, responded to, and monitored. New risks may emerge; realized threats become issues and require action through the appropriate control path.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: The register holds item-level risk detail. The Risk Management Plan governs the method; broader reporting may summarize aggregate exposure.

docs.title: Common Exam Confusions
docs.text:
• Treating an active issue as an uncertain future event.
  • Assuming risk work ends after planning.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text: A supplier-capacity risk records an early-warning trigger, owner, mitigation action, contingency, and the procurement decision that would follow if the trigger occurs.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: The Schedule Baseline provides the authorized timing commitment against which current performance is compared.

docs.title: Why It Exists
docs.text: Without a stable comparison point, a changing forecast can conceal variance and prevent disciplined change decisions.

docs.title: Created By
docs.text: • Develop Schedule

docs.title: Updated By
docs.text: • Perform Integrated Change Control after approval of a baseline-affecting change

docs.title: Used By
docs.text:
• Control Schedule
  • Monitor and Control Project Work

docs.title: Archived By
docs.text: • Close Project or Phase

docs.title: Contains
docs.text: Approved start and finish expectations, milestones, and the timing information selected for performance comparison.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text: The schedule model is analyzed and approved; the baseline is then compared with actual and forecast dates. Variance may prompt corrective action or a change request, not an automatic rebaseline.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: Current schedule information answers “what is now expected?” The baseline answers “what was authorized?”

docs.title: Common Exam Confusions
docs.text:
• Rebaselining whenever work slips.
  • Treating corrective action and baseline change as the same decision.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text: A forecast predicts a four-week delay. The baseline remains unchanged while the team evaluates recovery options and whether an authorized change is warranted.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: The Scope Baseline records the approved description and decomposition of project scope used for comparison and control.

docs.title: Why It Exists
docs.text: Delivery requires an agreed boundary. The baseline makes it possible to distinguish approved scope, elaboration within that scope, and proposed change.

docs.text: • Create WBS

docs.title: Updated By
docs.text: • Perform Integrated Change Control after an approved scope change

docs.title: Archived By

docs.text:
1. Approved project scope statement.
  2. Work breakdown structure.
  3. WBS dictionary.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text: Requirements inform the detailed scope; decomposition organizes that scope into manageable components; approval establishes the baseline; controlled changes create authorized revisions.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: The baseline defines approved scope. Requirements remain traceable, while schedule and cost baselines express authorized time and funding commitments.

docs.title: Common Exam Confusions
docs.text:
• Treating the WBS as a schedule.
  • Changing the baseline to hide variance.
  • Equating product scope with all project work.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text: A relocation project decomposes approved scope into site preparation, infrastructure, move execution, and readiness work packages, each clarified in the WBS dictionary.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Verified Deliverables are deliverables that have completed control-quality review and satisfy the defined quality criteria.

docs.title: Why It Exists
docs.text: The artifact exists because a deliverable should not be passed to acceptance activities unless it has been verified against the quality requirements defined earlier in the project.

docs.title: Created By
docs.text: • Control Quality

docs.title: Updated By
docs.text:
• Control Quality
  • Validate Scope

docs.title: Used By
docs.text:
• Validate Scope
  • Project sponsor or customer representatives

docs.title: Archived By
docs.text: • Project archive or knowledge management process

docs.title: Contains
docs.text:
• Deliverables that passed inspection or testing
  • Evidence of review outcomes
  • Related quality-control results

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text: Verified Deliverables are created after Control Quality confirms the work meets the applicable quality criteria and before formal acceptance through Validate Scope.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: Verified Deliverables result from Control Quality. They are submitted to Validate Scope for formal acceptance. They are distinct from Accepted Deliverables.

docs.title: Common Exam Confusions
docs.text:
• Treating Verified Deliverables as the same as Accepted Deliverables.
  • Assuming verification is the same as customer acceptance.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text: A completed software release passes the quality tests and becomes a verified deliverable before the customer reviews it for formal acceptance.

docs.title: Practical example and reusable resources
docs.text: The examples use the fictional ServiceBridge Modernization project so related artifacts share dates, budget, requirements, risks, issues, changes, deliverables, acceptance, transition, and benefits context.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Common across approaches. The verified deliverables keeps the same decision purpose; formality, storage, ownership, and update cadence are tailored to the work.

The filled example uses one shared structure. The comparison below explains how timing, ownership, detail, and cadence may still vary.

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text: Approach Typical timing and detail Ownership and approval Update cadence Predictive / Waterfall Planned earlier and detailed to the level needed for the approved end-to-end commitment. Central approval is common when a baseline, contract, or gate is affected. At control dates, reporting periods, and approved changes. Adaptive / Agile Refined near the work and release horizon; planning and documentation still occur. Teams and product roles decide within delegated boundaries; specialist and governance authority remains. Continuously, per iteration, or per release according to need. Hybrid Fixed obligations are detailed early while solution detail is progressively elaborated. Distributed delivery decisions connect to centralized decisions for baselines, contracts, compliance, and acceptance. Iteration-level updates plus integrated governance reviews.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Work Performance Information converts observed execution results into contextualized evidence about status, variance, trends, and likely outcomes.

docs.title: Why It Exists
docs.text: Raw observations do not explain significance. Analysis relates actual results to plans, baselines, thresholds, prior periods, dependencies, and forecasts.

docs.title: Created By
docs.text: Monitoring and controlling processes analyze relevant Work Performance Data within their domains.

docs.title: Updated By
docs.text: Each monitoring cycle refreshes applicable comparisons, trends, and forecasts.

docs.title: Used By

• Monitor and Control Project Work
  • Decision makers and communication processes

docs.title: Archived By

docs.title: Contains
docs.text:
1. Actual-versus-planned comparisons.
  2. Variance, trend, and forecast information.
  3. Threshold exceptions, causes, and decision context.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text: Execution produces data; domain controls analyze it into information; integrated monitoring selects and communicates decision-ready reports; decisions return as actions, changes, or updated plans.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: Work Performance Data are observations. Work Performance Information is analyzed context. Work Performance Reports are selected presentations for communication and decisions.

docs.title: Common Exam Confusions
docs.text:
• Using data, information, and reports as interchangeable labels.
  • Reporting variance without explaining its decision consequence.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text: Completed work, hours, defects, and dates are compared with baselines and thresholds to explain a worsening release trend and the decision required.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Work Performance Reports package relevant performance information for a defined audience and decision.

docs.title: Why It Exists
docs.text: Different stakeholders need different levels of detail, timing, and emphasis. Reports make integrated status understandable without replacing the underlying evidence.

docs.title: Created By

docs.title: Updated By

docs.text:
1. Reporting period and decision context.
  2. Selected status, variance, trend, forecast, risk, issue, and change information.

docs.title: Relationships

docs.title: Common Exam Confusions
docs.text:

  • Sending the same level of detail to every stakeholder.

docs.title: Decision Guides
docs.text:
Decision Guides start with a situation, not a process name. Use one when a scenario asks what should happen next, who can decide, what record must be updated, or when escalation is required.

A lifecycle chapter explains where work sits in the overall project story; a process page explains process mechanics; an artifact page explains a project record. A Decision Guide connects a current situation to authority → artifact → process or action → escalation without repeating those full references.

docs.title: How to use a guideQuality and AcceptanceRisk, Issues, and ImpedimentsChange and ComplianceProcurement, Transition, and ClosureBenefits
docs.text:
1. Match the facts of the scenario to the guide's current situation and immediate question.
  2. Identify the authority boundary before choosing an action.
  3. Update the relevant artifact or record and follow the applicable process or activity.
  4. Escalate only at the stated threshold, and check the common exam trap before deciding.

Decide what to do when technical verification or formal acceptance does not produce the expected result.

  • A Deliverable Fails Quality InspectionA completed deliverable fails an inspection or test and is not technically verified.
  • A Verified Deliverable Is Rejected During AcceptanceA technically verified deliverable is not accepted by the customer or designated acceptance authority.

Distinguish uncertainty from a current condition and decide when broader authority is required.

  • A Risk Occurs or an Impediment Exceeds Team AuthorityAn uncertain risk has occurred, or a blocker cannot be removed within team authority.

Route requested or required changes through the correct evidence and authority path.

  • A Stakeholder Requests a Baseline ChangeA stakeholder asks for work that may alter an approved scope, schedule, cost, or other controlled baseline.
  • A Compliance Problem Is DiscoveredTesting, audit, procurement, or operational readiness reveals a possible obligation failure.

Protect objectives and obligations when external delivery or readiness is threatened.

  • Seller Performance Threatens Project ObjectivesSeller delay, quality, capacity, or compliance performance threatens project commitments.
  • Transition or Closure Is Requested with Unresolved ObligationsTransition readiness is incomplete, or closure is requested while obligations, issues, procurement, or evidence remain unresolved.

Separate project closure from continuing operational benefits ownership and measurement.

  • Expected Benefits Are Not Yet Realized at Project ClosureOutputs are accepted and project closure is appropriate, but some expected benefits require later operational use or measurement.

docs.title: Expected Benefits Are Not Yet Realized at Project Closure
Current situation
docs.text: Outputs are accepted and project closure is appropriate, but some expected benefits require later operational use or measurement.

docs.title: Immediate question
docs.text: Is project work complete, and is continuing benefits ownership explicitly transferred?

docs.title: Applicable authority
docs.text: The closure authority decides project closure; the sponsor or governance model confirms the receiving benefit owner and review route.

docs.title: Relevant artifacts
docs.text:
• Benefits Management Information
  • Benefits Handoff Record
  • Transition Package
  • Formal Closure Record

docs.title: Correct process or activity
docs.text:
• Monitor and Control Project Work
  • Close Project or Phase

docs.title: Likely next action
docs.text: Confirm outputs and transition, document unrealized benefits and dependencies, obtain handoff acknowledgment, and close if authorized criteria are met.

docs.title: Escalation conditions
docs.text: Escalate when no benefit owner accepts the handoff, measures or data are missing, or closure criteria require additional project work.

docs.title: Common exam trap
docs.text: Keeping the project open indefinitely until every benefit occurs, or closing without a defined receiving owner.

docs.title: How to use this section
docs.text:
1. Read the assumption beside a formula before substituting values.
  2. Keep scope, status date, units, and calculation convention consistent.
  3. Use the interpretation to turn the result into a management question.

docs.title: Delivery-approach boundary
docs.text: Estimating applies across approaches, with differences in timing, granularity, and progressive elaboration. Network scheduling, approved baselines, and formal EVM are strongest in predictive and hybrid control structures. Adaptive delivery can estimate comparatively, elaborate detail just in time, and track iteration or release performance; formal EVM is possible only where suitable budget, scope, and performance-baseline measures exist. This does not imply every adaptive team uses EVM, or that adaptive work eliminates forecasting, budgeting, reserves, quality control, or schedule reasoning.

docs.title: Earned Value Management
docs.text:
Compare authorized planned value, budgeted value earned, and actual cost at one status date, then forecast using an explicit assumption.

PredictiveAdaptiveHybrid

docs.title: The three measures
docs.text:
PV — Planned Value: authorized budget assigned to work scheduled for completion by the status date.

EV — Earned Value: authorized budgeted value of work actually completed by the status date. A simple example may calculate EV as percent complete × budget for the measured work, but the measured budget may be a project, control account, work package, or other defined performance scope—EV is not merely “a percentage of BAC.”

AC — Actual Cost: actual cost incurred for the completed work by the status date.

BAC — Budget at Completion: approved cost baseline at completion for the measured scope.

!!! note "Schedule variance uses cost units" SV and CV use cost units because PV, EV, and AC are monetary budget values. SV is not directly a number of calendar days ahead or behind schedule.

docs.title: Formula reference
docs.text:
Verified · current 2026 courseFRM-EVM-001 Schedule variance

SV = EV - PV

PredictiveHybrid

Interpretation: Positive is ahead of planned value; zero is on plan; negative is behind planned value.

Assumptions: EV and PV cover the same measured scope and status date.

Units: Currency or other budget units.

SVschedule variance in cost unitsEVearned valuePVplanned value

Exam note: SV is expressed in cost units, not calendar days.

Verified · current 2026 courseFRM-EVM-002 Schedule performance index

SPI = EV / PV

PredictiveHybrid

Interpretation: Above 1 is ahead of planned value; 1 is on plan; below 1 is behind planned value.

Assumptions: PV is nonzero and scope/status date are aligned.

Units: Dimensionless ratio.

SPIschedule performance indexEVearned valuePVplanned value

Exam note: SPI does not prove a specific number of days ahead or behind.

Verified · current 2026 courseFRM-EVM-003 Cost variance

CV = EV - AC

PredictiveHybrid

Interpretation: Positive is under budget; zero is on budget; negative is over budget.

Assumptions: EV and AC cover the same measured scope and status date.

Units: Currency or other budget units.

CVcost varianceEVearned valueACactual cost

Exam note: Negative CV is unfavorable.

Verified · current 2026 courseFRM-EVM-004 Cost performance index

CPI = EV / AC

PredictiveHybrid

Interpretation: Above 1 is cost efficient; 1 is on budget; below 1 is cost inefficient.

Assumptions: AC is nonzero and scope/status date are aligned.

Units: Dimensionless ratio.

CPIcost performance indexEVearned valueACactual cost

Exam note: CPI below 1 means the project earns less budgeted value per unit of actual cost.

Verified · current 2026 courseFRM-EVM-005 Estimate at completion — current CPI continues

EAC = BAC / CPI

PredictiveHybrid

Interpretation: Forecasts total cost if current cost efficiency continues.

Assumptions: Current cumulative cost efficiency is expected to continue for the remaining work; CPI is nonzero.

Units: Currency.

EACforecast total cost at completionBACBudget at CompletionCPIcost performance index

Exam note: Choose an EAC formula by its assumption, not by memorized preference.

Verified · current 2026 courseFRM-EVM-006 Estimate to complete

ETC = EAC - AC

PredictiveHybrid

Interpretation: Forecasts cost remaining from the status date.

Assumptions: EAC and AC use the same measured scope and status date.

Units: Currency.

ETCforecast remaining costEACforecast total costACactual cost to date

Exam note: EAC is total forecast; ETC is remaining forecast.

Supplemental · official PMIFRM-EVM-007 EAC — remaining work at original rate

EAC = AC + (BAC - EV)

PredictiveHybrid

Interpretation: Adds actual cost to the original budget for uncompleted work.

Assumptions: Past variance is atypical and remaining work will perform at the original budgeted rate.

Units: Currency.

EACforecast total costACactual costBACBudget at CompletionEVearned value

Exam note: The assumption distinguishes this formula from BAC divided by CPI.

Verified · current 2026 courseFRM-EVM-008 EAC — cost and schedule influence remaining work

EAC = AC + ((BAC - EV) / (CPI × SPI))

PredictiveHybrid

Interpretation: Adjusts remaining work for both cost and schedule performance.

Assumptions: Both current cost and schedule performance are expected to influence remaining cost; CPI and SPI are nonzero.

Units: Currency.

EACforecast total costACactual costBACBudget at CompletionEVearned valueCPIcost performance indexSPIschedule performance index

Exam note: Use only when the question says both performance factors continue to affect remaining work.

Verified · current 2026 courseFRM-EVM-009 EAC — bottom-up remaining estimate

EAC = AC + bottom-up ETC

PredictiveHybrid

Interpretation: Replaces statistical extrapolation with a new detailed remaining-work estimate.

Assumptions: The original estimate is no longer reliable and the remaining work has been re-estimated.

Units: Currency.

EACforecast total costACactual costbottom-up ETCnew detailed estimate of remaining work

Exam note: Bottom-up ETC is an input from re-estimating, not a value derived from CPI.

Supplemental · official PMIFRM-EVM-010 Variance at completion

VAC = BAC - EAC

PredictiveHybrid

Interpretation: Positive forecasts under BAC; zero forecasts at BAC; negative forecasts over BAC.

Assumptions: BAC and EAC cover the same measured scope.

Units: Currency.

VACvariance at completionBACBudget at CompletionEACforecast total cost

Exam note: Supplemental coverage; do not assume equal course emphasis.

Supplemental · official PMIFRM-EVM-011 To-complete performance index against BAC

TCPI(BAC) = (BAC - EV) / (BAC - AC)

PredictiveHybrid

Interpretation: Efficiency the remaining work must achieve to meet BAC.

Assumptions: BAC minus AC is positive and BAC remains the selected target.

Units: Dimensionless ratio.

TCPIrequired future cost efficiencyBACBudget at CompletionEVearned valueACactual cost

Exam note: Compare the required efficiency with demonstrated performance for realism.

Supplemental · official PMIFRM-EVM-012 To-complete performance index against approved EAC

TCPI(EAC) = (BAC - EV) / (EAC - AC)

PredictiveHybrid

Interpretation: Efficiency the remaining work must achieve to meet the approved EAC target.

Assumptions: EAC minus AC is positive and EAC is the selected approved target.

Units: Dimensionless ratio.

TCPIrequired future cost efficiencyBACBudget at CompletionEVearned valueEACapproved forecast targetACactual cost

Exam note: The numerator remains budgeted work remaining; the denominator changes to funds remaining against EAC.

docs.title: EVM status-date chart
docs.text: ServiceBridge earned value status-date chartAt the status date, planned value is 1.2 million dollars, earned value is 1 million, and actual cost is 1.25 million. The planned curve continues toward BAC of 2.4 million.Status datePV $1.20MEV $1.00MAC $1.25MBAC $2.40M● PV planned■ EV earned▲ AC actualAt the status date, compare labels as well as line styles: EV is below PV while AC is above EV.

docs.title: ServiceBridge worked example
docs.text:
Inputs: BAC $2,400,000; PV $1,200,000; EV $1,000,000; AC $1,250,000.

Measure Result Meaning SV $-200,000 Less budgeted work completed than planned SPI 0.8333 Behind planned-value progress CV $-250,000 Actual cost exceeds earned value CPI 0.8000 $0.80 of budgeted value earned per $1.00 spent EAC = BAC / CPI $3,000,000 Forecast if current cost efficiency continues ETC $1,750,000 Forecast cost remaining VAC $-600,000 Supplemental forecast over BAC TCPI(BAC) 1.2174 Required remaining efficiency to meet BAC

The project has completed less budgeted work than planned and spent more than the budgeted value of completed work. If current cost performance continues, it is forecast to finish above BAC.

Formal EVM is strongest where predictive or hybrid control structures provide the necessary baseline measures. Adaptive delivery may use EVM at a release or other suitable performance-baseline level, but not every agile team uses formal EVM.

docs.title: Estimating
docs.text:
Choose an estimating method for the information available, document its assumptions, and refine it as knowledge improves.

PredictiveAdaptiveHybrid

docs.title: Four current-course techniques
docs.text:
Technique What it does Reliability condition Analogous / top-down estimating Uses historical information from a similar project or activity; it is usually faster and less costly, but less precise than detailed estimating. The comparison is meaningfully similar and relevant historical information is available. Parametric estimating Applies a measurable statistical relationship or unit rate, such as cost per square foot, hours per unit, or cost per transaction. The parameter is valid for the work and scales across the range being estimated. Three-point estimating Uses optimistic, most-likely, and pessimistic estimates to represent uncertainty rather than relying on one point. The three inputs describe the same scope, units, and conditions. Bottom-up estimating Estimates detailed activities, work packages, or lower-level components with people closest to the work, then aggregates upward. The decomposition is adequate and component estimates use compatible units and scope boundaries.

!!! note "Top-down is not a fifth peer technique" In this course family, analogous estimating is also described as top-down estimating. Beginning with a fixed funding limit and asking what can be delivered is a top-down budgeting or scope-allocation decision—not a separate fifth estimating technique.

docs.title: Formula reference
docs.text:
Verified · current 2026 courseFRM-EST-001 Parametric estimate

Estimate = Quantity × Rate per unit

PredictiveAdaptiveHybrid

Interpretation: Multiplies a valid unit relationship by the measured quantity.

Assumptions: The rate is valid and scalable for the quantity and conditions.

Units: Output uses the rate numerator unit; quantity and rate denominator must match.

Estimateestimated duration or costQuantitynumber of unitsRateduration or cost per unit

Exam note: Test the parameter's validity before applying the arithmetic.

Verified · current 2026 courseFRM-EST-002 Triangular three-point estimate

TE = (O + M + P) / 3

PredictiveAdaptiveHybrid

Interpretation: Gives equal weight to all three estimates.

Assumptions: O, M, and P use the same scope and units.

Units: Same time, effort, or cost unit as O, M, and P.

TEexpected estimateOoptimistic estimateMmost-likely estimatePpessimistic estimate

Exam note: Keep the entire numerator in parentheses.

Verified · current 2026 courseFRM-EST-003 Beta / PERT three-point estimate

TE = (O + 4M + P) / 6

PredictiveAdaptiveHybrid

Interpretation: Weights the most-likely estimate four times as heavily.

Assumptions: O, M, and P use the same scope and units and a beta approximation is appropriate.

Units: Same time, effort, or cost unit as O, M, and P.

TEexpected estimateOoptimistic estimateMmost-likely estimatePpessimistic estimate

Exam note: The coefficient 4 applies only to M.

Verified · official PMIFRM-EST-004 PERT standard deviation

σ = (P - O) / 6

PredictiveHybrid

Interpretation: Approximates dispersion around the PERT mean.

Assumptions: The PERT beta approximation and comparable endpoints are appropriate.

Units: Same unit as P and O.

σstandard deviationPpessimistic estimateOoptimistic estimate

Exam note: This is dispersion in the estimate's unit, not a guaranteed range.

docs.title: Worked comparison
docs.text:
For a duration with O = 8 days, M = 12 days, and P = 20 days, the triangular estimate is 13.33 days, the beta/PERT estimate is 12.67 days, and the verified PERT standard deviation is 2 days. The PERT result is closer to the most-likely estimate because M receives four times the weight.

A parametric example: 320 records at 1.5 hours per record produces 480 hours, provided the rate remains valid at that volume.

docs.title: Adaptive and hybrid treatment
docs.text: Adaptive teams may estimate comparatively or at several horizons and elaborate detail just in time. Those are general adaptive practices; story points are not universal, and Scrum- or Kanban-specific techniques should not be generalized to every adaptive approach.

docs.title: Reserves and Baselines
docs.text:
Separate estimated work, identified uncertainty, the approved cost baseline, and governance-controlled management reserve.

PredictiveAdaptiveHybrid

docs.title: Budget relationship
docs.text:
Verified · current 2026 courseFRM-RES-001 Cost baseline / BAC

BAC = aggregated cost estimates + contingency reserves

PredictiveHybrid

Interpretation: BAC includes contingency reserve and excludes management reserve.

Assumptions: Scope and reserve treatment are authorized under project governance.

Units: Currency.

BACBudget at Completion and approved cost baselineaggregated cost estimatesapproved component estimatescontingency reservesbudget for identified uncertainty

Exam note: BAC means Budget at Completion, not Budgeted at Completion.

Verified · current 2026 courseFRM-RES-002 Total project budget

Total Project Budget = BAC + management reserve

PredictiveHybrid

Interpretation: Management reserve sits outside BAC but inside total project budget.

Assumptions: Management reserve is governed and not used for unauthorized out-of-scope work.

Units: Currency.

Total Project Budgetauthorized project budget including management reserveBACapproved cost baselinemanagement reservebudget for unforeseen in-scope work

Exam note: Moving management reserve into the baseline requires the applicable authorization.

Budget and reserves stack — management reserve is outside BAC. Aggregated cost estimates $2.20M + Contingency reserve $0.20M = BAC / cost baseline $2.40M + Management reserve $0.15M = Total project budget $2.55M

docs.title: Distinctions
docs.text:
BAC — Budget at Completion is the total approved cost baseline for the measured scope. It includes contingency reserve within the baseline and excludes management reserve.

Contingency reserve addresses identified uncertainty or known unknowns and may relate to identified risks or expected variability. It is part of the cost baseline.

Management reserve addresses unforeseen work or unknown unknowns within project scope. It is outside the cost baseline and BAC, but inside total project budget. It does not authorize out-of-scope work.

Formal baseline and reserve structures are strongest in predictive and hybrid governance. Adaptive delivery still budgets and forecasts; it may manage uncertainty at release or other suitable horizons.

docs.title: Schedule Analysis
docs.text:
Build the network first, then calculate dates, float, and the path that governs the earliest modeled completion.

PredictiveAdaptiveHybrid

docs.title: Calculation convention
docs.text:
The Atlas begins the first activity at time zero: EF = ES + duration; a successor ES is the maximum predecessor EF; LS = LF - duration; and a predecessor LF is the minimum successor LS.

!!! warning "Exam numbering convention" Some course diagrams use inclusive day numbering and apply +1 or -1 adjustments. Follow the convention shown in the question. Do not mix conventions within one calculation.

docs.title: Formula reference
docs.text:
Verified · official PMIFRM-SCH-001 Early finish

EF = ES + Duration

PredictiveHybrid

Interpretation: Calculates earliest finish in the Atlas day-zero convention.

Assumptions: Finish-to-start logic without lag unless the network states otherwise.

Units: Consistent time units.

EFearliest finishESearliest startDurationactivity duration

Exam note: Inclusive-day diagrams may use +1 or -1; follow the question's convention.

Verified · official PMIFRM-SCH-002 Late start

LS = LF - Duration

PredictiveHybrid

Interpretation: Calculates latest start in the Atlas day-zero convention.

Assumptions: The required finish and successor logic are established.

Units: Consistent time units.

LSlatest startLFlatest finishDurationactivity duration

Exam note: Use the smallest successor late-start value at convergence.

Verified · current 2026 courseFRM-SCH-003 Total float from start dates

Total Float = LS - ES

PredictiveHybrid

Interpretation: Zero normally identifies critical work under the chosen convention.

Assumptions: Early and late dates use the same convention and calendars.

Units: Time units.

Total Floattime available before project completion is delayedLSlatest startESearliest start

Exam note: More than one zero-float critical path may exist.

Verified · current 2026 courseFRM-SCH-004 Total float from finish dates

Total Float = LF - EF

PredictiveHybrid

Interpretation: Equivalent to LS minus ES when conventions are consistent.

Assumptions: Early and late dates use the same convention and calendars.

Units: Time units.

Total Floattime available before project completion is delayedLFlatest finishEFearliest finish

Exam note: Do not mix inclusive and day-zero calculations.

Verified · official PMIFRM-SCH-005 Free float

Free Float = earliest ES of immediate successors - EF

PredictiveHybrid

Interpretation: Measures flexibility before the next activity's early start is affected.

Assumptions: Use the earliest ES when there are multiple immediate successors.

Units: Time units.

Free Floattime available before an immediate successor is delayedESearliest start of a successorEFearliest finish of the current activity

Exam note: Free float protects successor early starts; total float protects project completion.

docs.title: Critical path and float
docs.text:
The critical path is the longest-duration path through the network and determines the shortest calculated project duration. Critical-path activities normally have zero total float under the selected convention; more than one critical path may exist. A noncritical delay changes completion only after available float is exhausted or the critical path changes.

A · Confirm scope

Duration 3 days · predecessor none

ES0EF3LS0LF3TF0 B · Configure service

Duration 5 days · predecessor A

ES3EF8LS3LF8TF0 C · Prepare training

Duration 3 days · predecessor A

ES3EF6LS5LF8TF2 D · Validate release

Duration 4 days · predecessor B, C

ES8EF12LS8LF12TF0

Result: A → B → D is the 12-day critical path. C has two days of total float. The labels and table values—not color alone—identify critical work.

docs.title: Compression and resource optimization
docs.text:
Technique Primary constraint Likely cost effect Schedule effect Key risk Fast tracking Dependency flexibility Usually neutral directly Shortens when overlap is feasible Rework and coordination Crashing Critical-path duration Usually increases Shortens only if critical work changes Cost, risk, complexity Resource smoothing Available float Usually limited Completion unchanged May leave overallocations Resource leveling Resource availability May increase May extend or change critical path Milestone delay

Crashing is broader than simply adding people: it may use resources, spending, procurement, technology, or another cost-bearing intervention. It must reduce critical-path duration to shorten project completion.

docs.title: Shared Knowledge and Authority
docs.text: This page owns recurring roles, delivery terminology, issue distinctions, compliance traceability, and benefits handoff. Process pages retain context-specific authority; the structured quantitative-method registry owns the schedule, estimating, reserves, and earned-value formula family.

docs.title: Potential communication channels
docs.text:
Status: Verified

Expression: n(n - 1) / 2

n is the number of potential participants; the result counts pairwise paths and does not prescribe a communication plan.

docs.title: Sponsor
docs.text:
Champions the initiative and connects it to authorization, funding, direction, and escalation authority.

Authority boundary: Exact approval rights depend on governance; sponsor does not automatically mean customer or benefits owner.

docs.title: Project Manager
docs.text:
Integrates project work, information, and decisions within delegated authority.

Authority boundary: Escalates matters outside project authority rather than assuming specialist or sponsor rights.

docs.title: Product Owner
docs.text:
In product-oriented adaptive contexts, orders value-focused work and makes product decisions within the governing model.

Authority boundary: Scrum-specific accountability is not generalized to every adaptive approach or formal acceptance.

docs.title: Customer or Acceptance Authority
docs.text:
Formally accepts verified deliverables or scope results under the applicable agreement or governance model.

Authority boundary: Technical verification and formal acceptance are separate decisions.

docs.title: Team
docs.text:
Performs and coordinates work, contributes estimates and evidence, and resolves matters within team authority.

Authority boundary: Self-management does not erase external governance, compliance, procurement, or acceptance limits.

docs.title: Governance Body
docs.text:
Provides organizational direction and decisions under the initiative's governance model.

Authority boundary: Its exact mandate for funding, baselines, exceptions, continuation, or closure is organization-specific.

docs.title: Change Authority or CCB
docs.text:
Evaluates and disposes controlled changes within an approved mandate.

Authority boundary: Thresholds and whether a standing board is needed are tailored.

docs.title: Benefit Owner
docs.text:
Owns defined benefit measures, dependencies, reviews, and continuing action after explicit handoff.

Authority boundary: The project manager does not universally retain this role after closure.

docs.title: Operational Owner
docs.text:
Accepts operational responsibility for transferred outputs, support, controls, and residual obligations.

Authority boundary: Transfer may require evidence from technical, security, quality, and compliance authorities.

docs.title: Quality, Compliance, Procurement, and Risk Authorities
docs.text:
Exercise specialist review or decision rights within organizational and contractual mandates.

Authority boundary: These roles are not interchangeable and may be advisory, approving, auditing, or controlling.

docs.title: Delivery-approach terminology
docs.text:
• Predictive: Establishes a comparatively broad authorized plan and baselines when work can be usefully defined in advance; iteration still occurs.
  • Adaptive: Uses short planning and delivery horizons with frequent review when learning and change are expected.
  • Hybrid: Deliberately combines cadences or governance models and defines how their evidence and decisions reconnect.
  • Scrum: A specific framework with defined accountabilities, events, and artifacts; not a synonym for adaptive delivery.
  • Kanban: A flow-oriented method using visualization, WIP control, pull, and flow measures; not a synonym for every adaptive board.

docs.title: Risks, issues, and impediments
docs.text:
• Risk: An uncertain event or condition that can affect objectives.
  • Realized Risk: A risk occurrence becomes a current condition and may create or update an issue.
  • Issue: A current condition requiring action, ownership, and possibly escalation or change.
  • Impediment: A blocker or flow constraint that may remain team-level or become an issue when broader action or traceability is needed.

docs.title: Compliance trace
docs.text:
The migration preserves this trace without claiming a universal compliance framework.

  1. Requirements and obligation source
  2. Scope and acceptance criteria
  3. Risk identification and response
  4. Quality controls and test evidence
  5. Procurement statements, criteria, and agreements
  6. Evidence, findings, and audits
  7. Formal acceptance
  8. Transition, retention, and closure

docs.title: Benefits handoff
docs.text:
• Project work produces outputs and can enable outcomes; it does not guarantee or indefinitely own benefit realization.
  • Formal closure may occur before every intended benefit is realized.
  • Continuing measurement requires an identified benefit owner, measures, data, dates, dependencies, and escalation route.
  • The receiving governance model is organization-specific and is not invented by the Atlas. Formula and Quantitative Methods is the public, generated study reference for the verified quantitative family.

docs.title: Project Start to Completion
docs.text:
Project Lifecycle Guide

Project Start to Completion

A relational route through project conditions, decisions, handoffs, concurrent work, and feedback—from an observed need to formal closure and continuing benefits ownership.

Recurring role, authority, delivery-approach, issue, compliance, and benefits terms use the Shared Knowledge and Authority reference.

docs.title: Lifecycle phases are not process groups
docs.text:
A project lifecycle describes how the project and its results change state over time. PMI process groups classify management activity by purpose: initiating, planning, executing, monitoring and controlling, and closing. Those purposes can recur within a phase, release, iteration, or workstream. They are not five consecutive project phases.

Planning continues as uncertainty is reduced. Execution produces information that monitoring interprets. Risk, quality, stakeholder engagement, communications, knowledge, and change work cross most of the lifecycle. Closing can apply to a phase or terminated effort as well as to the entire project.

docs.title: End-to-end sequence
docs.text:
1. Business need and intended value establish why action may be warranted.
  2. Authorization creates a recognized project or phase with accountable sponsorship.
  3. Stakeholder identification reveals affected people, expectations, influence, and decision authority.
  4. Delivery approach and governance establish cadence, controls, roles, and escalation.
  5. Integrated and detailed planning reconcile scope, schedule, cost, quality, resources, communications, risk, procurement, and engagement.
  6. Authorized execution coordinates people and resources to create deliverables.
  7. Deliverables and performance information provide results and evidence for control.
  8. Monitoring, issue resolution, and change decisions compare conditions with intent and authorize responses.
  9. Verification confirms that completed deliverables meet defined quality requirements.
  10. Formal acceptance records the authorized stakeholder's decision.
  11. Transition moves accepted results and operating responsibility to the receiving environment.
  12. Closure completes administrative, contractual, knowledge, archive, and release work.
  13. Continuing benefits ownership and measurement remain with a designated post-project owner; the exact relationship to formal closure remains a documented source conflict.

docs.title: How delivery approaches change the route
docs.text: Predictive work tends to authorize broader baselines before major execution. Adaptive work uses shorter planning-and-delivery cycles, a prioritized work queue, frequent review, and continuing refinement. Hybrid work deliberately assigns different components or governance levels to different cadences. None removes the need to establish purpose, authority, quality, risk treatment, stakeholder feedback, decision rights, acceptance, and responsible transition.
