docs.title: Verification, Acceptance, Transition, and Closure
docs.text:
Lifecycle chapter 10

Verification, Acceptance, Transition, and Closure

Finishing production is not the end: results must be verified, accepted by the proper authority, transitioned responsibly, and closed with ownership intact.

Lifecycle orientation

docs.title: Process Phases
docs.text:
These process groups overlap and repeat; the emphasis shows where this chapter most often concentrates.

  1. InitiatingProcess group
  2. PlanningProcess group
  3. ExecutingProcess group · emphasized
  4. Monitoring and ControllingProcess group · emphasized
  5. ClosingProcess group · emphasized

docs.title: Local sequence
docs.text:
1. Submit completed deliverables to Control Quality for inspection and testing.
  2. Move conforming work to Verified Deliverables; return failed work through defect analysis and authorized correction.
  3. Present verified deliverables to the authorized acceptance role through Validate Scope or the applicable equivalent.
  4. Record Accepted Deliverables or route rejected work through clarification, correction, or change.
  5. Confirm outstanding work, obligations, risks, issues, agreements, and readiness before transition.
  6. Transfer accepted results, operating knowledge, support information, access, and accountable ownership.
  7. Finalize lessons, reports, archives, procurement obligations, resources, and formal project or phase closure.
  8. Hand benefits information and measurement responsibility to the designated post-project owner without silently claiming that all benefits are already realized.

docs.title: Handoffs
docs.text:
What enters

Completed and verified deliverables, acceptance conditions, agreements, open items, readiness evidence, knowledge, and business intent.

What this work accomplishes

Establishes conformance, formal acceptance, operational responsibility, defensible completion, preserved knowledge, and explicit continuing ownership.

What moves next

Accepted results and operating responsibility transfer; closure records are archived; unresolved benefit measurement moves to its designated owner.

docs.title: Rejection, early termination, and authority
docs.text:
Failed verification returns to correction or authorized disposition before acceptance. Rejected acceptance returns through analysis and the applicable decision route. Transition readiness gaps can delay handoff or require a controlled exception. A terminated project still requires orderly closure of obligations, records, knowledge, contracts, and resources.

Quality control verifies. The designated customer, sponsor, product, or receiving role accepts. Operational owners confirm readiness and receive responsibility. Procurement authority closes agreement obligations. The sponsor or authorized governance role confirms formal project or phase closure according to the governing model.

docs.title: Benefits conflict preserved
docs.text:
The repository's current primary-source registry supports formal completion, transition, and archival relationships but does not resolve when benefit realization defines project completion. The Confluence source states that benefit measurement may continue after formal closure; the existing Master Project Sequence previously stated that the project is complete only when intended value is realized.

This guide therefore preserves the conflict rather than claiming either rule as verified. It distinguishes formal project closure from continuing benefits ownership, requires an explicit handoff, and leaves the exact post-project authority model deferred pending current PMI or framework verification.

docs.title: Approach treatment and exam distinctions
docs.text:
Predictive closure may consolidate a broad final release or phase. Adaptive and hybrid work may transition increments earlier, but still need final project-level obligations, archives, resources, and authority addressed. Acceptance is not verification, transition is not acceptance, and completion of production is not formal closure.

docs.title: Adaptive and Hybrid Delivery
docs.text:
Lifecycle chapter 9

Adaptive and Hybrid Delivery

Adaptive and hybrid approaches alter how often work is planned, built, reviewed, and accepted; they do not eliminate purpose, risk, quality, governance, or accountability.

Lifecycle orientation

docs.title: Process Phases
docs.text:
These process groups overlap and repeat; the emphasis shows where this chapter most often concentrates.

  1. InitiatingProcess group
  2. PlanningProcess group · emphasized
  3. ExecutingProcess group · emphasized
  4. Monitoring and ControllingProcess group · emphasized
  5. ClosingProcess group

docs.title: Local adaptive loop
docs.text:
1. Maintain an outcome-oriented vision and prioritized work queue.
  2. Refine enough detail for the next planning horizon and agree acceptance conditions.
  3. Select work within capacity and explicit working agreements.
  4. Build, integrate, test, and make completed results visible.
  5. Review outcomes with stakeholders and capture evidence.
  6. Improve the product, process, priorities, and plans through feedback.
  7. Repeat while maintaining governance, compliance, risk, funding, and transition visibility.

docs.title: Handoffs
docs.text:
What enters

Vision, value hypotheses, constraints, prioritized needs, capacity, quality expectations, risks, and stakeholder feedback.

What this work accomplishes

Reduces uncertainty through short learning cycles and delivers inspectable results at a sustainable cadence.

What moves next

Accepted increments, evidence, learning, changed priorities, emerging risks, and improvement actions enter the next cycle or transition.

docs.title: Predictive, adaptive, and hybrid distinctions
docs.text:
Predictive approaches seek more integrated definition before broad execution when scope and path can be planned usefully. Adaptive approaches intentionally defer detail and use frequent feedback when uncertainty or change is high. Hybrid approaches assign different components, layers, or decisions to different cadences for an explicit reason.

Hybrid does not mean using inconsistent terminology or duplicating governance. It must state where priorities can change, where contracts or baselines constrain change, how evidence crosses boundaries, and who resolves conflicts between delivery systems.

docs.title: Roles, quality, risk, and change
docs.text:
Adaptive role labels vary by framework and organization. This guide uses function-first language—sponsor or governance authority, outcome or product direction, delivery facilitation, team ownership, stakeholder acceptance—so role authority does not drift across pages. Framework-specific authority claims remain source-limited until current primary references are registered.

Quality is built into working agreements and completion criteria, then supported by verification and acceptance evidence. Risks are reviewed continuously. Feedback can reprioritize work within delegated guardrails; changes outside those guardrails follow the applicable governance path.

docs.title: Business environment and continuous improvement
docs.text: External regulation, market conditions, technology, suppliers, and internal strategy or capability can change the viable approach. The team observes those conditions, evaluates their impact, and adapts through authorized decisions. Improvement actions should name an owner and affect the next working cycle rather than remain retrospective notes.

docs.title: Exam distinctions
docs.text:
Adaptive does not mean no planning or documentation. A backlog item is not automatically approved scope under every governance model. Review, verification, and acceptance are related but distinct decisions. Velocity or flow measures support forecasting and improvement; they are not universal productivity scores.

docs.title: Conception and Authorization
docs.text:
Lifecycle chapter 1

Conception and Authorization

The project begins when evidence, sponsorship, authority, stakeholder understanding, and an initial delivery approach are connected—not merely when someone proposes work.

Lifecycle orientation

docs.title: Process Phases
docs.text:
These process groups overlap and repeat; the emphasis shows where this chapter most often concentrates.

  1. InitiatingProcess group · emphasized
  2. PlanningProcess group
  3. ExecutingProcess group
  4. Monitoring and ControllingProcess group
  5. ClosingProcess group

docs.title: Local sequence
docs.text:
1. Recognize a problem, opportunity, obligation, or strategic need.
  2. Evaluate whether a project response is justified; keep detailed business-case mechanics with the originating organization until a verified artifact owner exists.
  3. Describe intended outcomes and benefits without claiming they have already been realized.
  4. Establish agreements or constraints that precede authorization when applicable.
  5. Approve the Project Charter through the appropriate sponsor authority.
  6. Identify Stakeholders and record influence, needs, impact, and engagement information.
  7. Select and tailor a workable delivery approach and establish decision rights.

docs.title: Handoffs
docs.text:
What enters

Need evidence, strategy, constraints, agreements, initial risks, intended outcomes, and decision criteria.

What this work accomplishes

Turns an idea into an authorized, governable effort and reveals who can affect or accept its results.

What moves next

Charter, initial assumptions, stakeholder information, delivery approach, and governance expectations enter integrated planning.

docs.title: Roles and authority
docs.text: The sponsor or authorized initiating body approves the project and establishes high-level authority. The project manager supports development of the charter and organizes the authorized work; this role does not self-authorize the project. Stakeholders supply needs, constraints, expertise, influence, and acceptance expectations. Governance roles define which decisions may be made locally and which require escalation.

docs.title: Feedback and approach treatment
docs.text:
Planning may reveal that the original case is infeasible, a key stakeholder was omitted, or the proposed delivery approach does not fit the uncertainty. That information returns to the sponsor for clarification, tailoring, reauthorization, deferral, or termination.

Predictive work often establishes broader boundaries early. Adaptive work may authorize an outcome and funding guardrails while allowing scope detail to emerge through short feedback cycles. Hybrid work must state which decisions are fixed, which evolve, and who controls the boundary between them.

docs.title: Artifact states and exam distinctions
docs.text:
Need evidence supports a decision; it is not authorization. A draft charter becomes an authorization record only through approval. Stakeholder information begins early and continues to change. Delivery-approach selection is a tailoring decision, not permission to omit management purposes.

For exam reasoning, separate the business case from the charter, the sponsor's authorization from the project manager's management authority, and stakeholder identification from the later work of planning and managing engagement.

docs.title: Execution and Team Leadership
docs.text:
Lifecycle chapter 7

Execution and Team Leadership

Execution is concurrent coordination: the team creates results while learning, communicating, engaging, resolving conflict, implementing responses, and producing performance evidence.

Lifecycle orientation

docs.title: Process Phases
docs.text:
These process groups overlap and repeat; the emphasis shows where this chapter most often concentrates.

  1. InitiatingProcess group
  2. PlanningProcess group
  3. ExecutingProcess group · emphasized
  4. Monitoring and ControllingProcess group · emphasized
  5. ClosingProcess group

docs.title: Local sequence
docs.text:
1. Confirm authorized work, near-term priorities, resources, decision rights, and working agreements.
  2. Direct and manage project work to create deliverables and work performance data.
  3. Acquire, develop, and support the team; address conflict at the appropriate level.
  4. Manage knowledge so experience can improve present work and future decisions.
  5. Perform quality, communications, risk-response, procurement, and stakeholder-engagement work concurrently.
  6. Route issues, impediments, defects, new risks, and proposed changes into their controlled decision paths.

docs.title: Handoffs
docs.text:
What enters

Authorized plans and changes, resources, stakeholder expectations, agreements, risk responses, and quality criteria.

What this work accomplishes

Creates deliverables, team capability, communications, knowledge, implemented responses, and observed performance.

What moves next

Completed work enters verification; data enters domain controls; issues and changes enter decisions; learning returns to current plans.

docs.title: Leadership, conflict, and feedback
docs.text:
The project manager integrates work and removes organizational friction within delegated authority. Team members own assigned work and contribute expertise. Functional managers or resource owners retain relevant people authority. Sponsors and governance bodies resolve escalated direction or funding decisions. Stakeholders participate through the planned engagement routes.

Conflict is information about competing needs, constraints, or behavior. Resolve it at the lowest responsible level that has authority and context; escalate when safety, ethics, compliance, contractual limits, or delegated authority require it. An impediment should have an owner and path to removal even though the repository does not yet have a source-verified canonical impediment artifact page.

docs.title: Approach treatment and artifact states
docs.text:
Predictive execution coordinates against approved work packages and plans. Adaptive execution selects near-term items, collaborates through short cycles, demonstrates increments, and learns from feedback. Hybrid execution must keep cross-cadence dependencies and decision rights visible.

Work performance data are observations from execution. They become Work Performance Information only after analysis. Completed deliverables are not verified or accepted merely because the team finished production.

docs.title: Exam distinctions
docs.text:
Approved changes are implemented; proposed changes are not. Manage Project Knowledge is continuous rather than a final archive task. Team development and team management are related but distinct. Servant leadership does not remove accountability, governance, or escalation.

docs.title: Integrated Planning
docs.text:
Lifecycle chapter 2

Integrated Planning

Planning becomes usable when its parts agree about scope, timing, funding, quality, people, uncertainty, information, authority, and change.

Lifecycle orientation

docs.title: Process Phases
docs.text:
These process groups overlap and repeat; the emphasis shows where this chapter most often concentrates.

  1. InitiatingProcess group
  2. PlanningProcess group · emphasized
  3. ExecutingProcess group
  4. Monitoring and ControllingProcess group
  5. ClosingProcess group

docs.title: Local sequence
docs.text:
1. Use the charter and stakeholder information to establish planning boundaries.
  2. Develop detailed subsidiary approaches and baselines through the relevant planning processes.
  3. Plan stakeholder engagement, resources, team working agreements, and communications.
  4. Define how changes, configuration items, versions, approvals, and records will be controlled.
  5. Reconcile contradictions across scope, schedule, cost, quality, risk, resources, procurement, and stakeholder expectations.
  6. Approve the integrated Project Management Plan and establish shared understanding before authorized execution.

docs.title: Handoffs
docs.text:
What enters

Authorization, assumptions, stakeholder information, enterprise constraints, organizational assets, and emerging detailed plans.

What this work accomplishes

Creates coherent management direction, usable decision thresholds, information routes, and an agreed basis for action.

What moves next

Approved plans and baselines guide execution; working documents and forecasts continue to evolve within those controls.

docs.title: Concurrent planning and return loops
docs.text: Detailed planning is concurrent and iterative. Scope influences schedule and cost; resources constrain duration; risks affect reserves and responses; procurement timing affects schedule; quality and compliance criteria affect acceptance. A contradiction returns to the affected planning owners before approval. Execution evidence later returns through monitoring and may trigger replanning or formal change.

docs.title: Roles, authority, and approaches
docs.text:
The project manager integrates planning and makes conflicts visible. Subject-matter owners develop relevant components. The sponsor or governance body resolves decisions outside delegated authority. Team members and stakeholders contribute practical knowledge and commitment.

Predictive planning commonly develops more of the integrated direction before major execution. Adaptive planning establishes vision, guardrails, cadence, working agreements, and enough detail for the next horizon. Hybrid planning must explicitly reconcile rolling detail with any predictive milestones, contracts, compliance gates, or baselines.

docs.title: Artifact states and exam distinctions
docs.text:
Working drafts are progressively integrated, then approved. Once controlled, a changed forecast or document does not automatically change a baseline. A kickoff communicates and aligns around approved direction; it is not a substitute for integration or authorization.

The communication-channel formula and other formulas remain with their process or future verified formula owner; this chapter does not duplicate them.

docs.title: Monitoring and Change
docs.text:
Lifecycle chapter 8

Monitoring and Change

Monitoring explains what current evidence means; change control decides what authorized direction should change.

Lifecycle orientation

docs.title: Process Phases
docs.text:
These process groups overlap and repeat; the emphasis shows where this chapter most often concentrates.

  1. InitiatingProcess group
  2. PlanningProcess group
  3. ExecutingProcess group · emphasized
  4. Monitoring and ControllingProcess group · emphasized
  5. ClosingProcess group

docs.title: Local sequence
docs.text:
1. Capture work performance data from execution and relevant external conditions.
  2. Analyze domain results into Work Performance Information.
  3. Integrate status, variance, trends, forecasts, risks, issues, and dependencies through Monitor and Control Project Work.
  4. Communicate decision-ready Work Performance Reports.
  5. Resolve issues within delegated authority or escalate through the named governance route.
  6. Document proposed changes as Change Requests, analyze impacts, and obtain an authorized disposition.
  7. Implement approved changes, update controlled records, and verify the resulting work.

docs.title: Handoffs and return loops
docs.text:
What enters

Actual results, forecasts, defects, risks, issues, stakeholder feedback, agreement performance, and current plans.

What this work accomplishes

Creates integrated understanding and authorized responses while preserving configuration and decision history.

What moves next

Actions return to execution; approved changes update affected owners; rejected requests leave baselines unchanged; verified results proceed to acceptance.

Control is continuous. A defect can return to correction and reinspection. A variance can prompt analysis, corrective action, or change. A new issue can reveal a risk response failure. Stakeholder feedback can require engagement adjustment without necessarily changing scope. Every return path needs an owner and an authority boundary.

docs.title: Issues, impediments, and configuration
docs.text:
An issue is a current condition requiring action; a risk is uncertain. An impediment blocks or slows progress and may be an issue, organizational constraint, dependency, or policy concern. The lifecycle guide makes these relationships explicit, but dedicated issue-log and impediment destinations remain deferred because current repository sources do not yet support responsible standalone pages.

Version and configuration controls preserve which approved artifact state applies. A changed working document, an approved change, and an updated baseline are different events.

docs.title: Approach treatment and exam distinctions
docs.text:
Predictive control often compares performance with broader baselines. Adaptive control uses frequent review of outcomes, flow, quality, and feedback within governance guardrails. Hybrid control must integrate both evidence types without forcing one cadence to masquerade as the other.

Data, information, and reports are not interchangeable. Corrective action is not automatic baseline change. Only the authorized role or body may approve a controlled change. Approved change implementation must be verified.

docs.title: Quality
docs.text:
Lifecycle chapter 5

Quality

Quality connects requirements to planned criteria, capable processes, inspection evidence, verified deliverables, and acceptance decisions.

Lifecycle orientation

docs.title: Process Phases
docs.text:
These process groups overlap and repeat; the emphasis shows where this chapter most often concentrates.

  1. InitiatingProcess group
  2. PlanningProcess group · emphasized
  3. ExecutingProcess group · emphasized
  4. Monitoring and ControllingProcess group · emphasized
  5. ClosingProcess group

docs.title: Local sequence
docs.text:
1. Use requirements, traceability, scope, risk, stakeholder, and compliance information to plan quality.
  2. Create the Quality Management Plan and Quality Metrics.
  3. Apply the planned approach during execution and improve process capability through Manage Quality.
  4. Inspect or test completed deliverables through Control Quality and record Quality-Control Measurements.
  5. Move conforming results to Verified Deliverables.
  6. Submit verified deliverables for formal acceptance, producing Accepted Deliverables when authorized acceptance is granted.

docs.title: Handoffs and return loops
docs.text:
What enters

Requirements, acceptance conditions, scope, standards, regulations, risk, stakeholder expectations, and lessons.

What this work accomplishes

Defines measurable quality, improves delivery processes, and produces evidence about deliverable conformance.

What moves next

Verified deliverables enter acceptance; defects, trends, and process findings return to execution, risk, planning, or change.

Failed inspection does not become acceptance. The team analyzes the defect, determines the authorized response, performs correction or change work, and reinspects. A stakeholder rejection after verification is different: it may reveal an expectation, scope, requirement, or acceptance problem and follows the quality inspection failure decision guide as applicable.

docs.title: Roles, authority, and approaches
docs.text:
The project manager ensures integration. Quality specialists and the delivery team plan and perform quality work. Control Quality verifies conformance. The designated customer or sponsor role accepts; quality personnel do not silently substitute for that authority.

Predictive work may establish broader criteria and planned reviews before production. Adaptive work embeds criteria, review, testing, and feedback in each increment. Hybrid work must maintain consistent evidence and acceptance authority across both cadences.

docs.title: Exam distinctions
docs.text:
Manage Quality concerns the effectiveness and improvement of processes; Control Quality concerns results and conformance evidence. Verification precedes acceptance. Grade and quality are different concepts. Commercial audit or template examples are illustrations, not PMI-prescribed formats; detailed audit claims remain source-limited where the registry lacks current primary verification.

docs.title: Requirements and Scope
docs.text:
Lifecycle chapter 3

Requirements and Scope

Needs become controllable when they can be traced through scope, decomposition, delivery, verification, and formal acceptance.

Lifecycle orientation

docs.title: Process Phases
docs.text:
These process groups overlap and repeat; the emphasis shows where this chapter most often concentrates.

  1. InitiatingProcess group
  2. PlanningProcess group · emphasized
  3. ExecutingProcess group
  4. Monitoring and ControllingProcess group · emphasized
  5. ClosingProcess group

docs.title: Local sequence
docs.text:
1. Plan how requirements and scope will be developed, validated, and controlled.
  2. Elicit and analyze needs into Requirements Documentation.
  3. Connect requirements to origin and downstream evidence in the Requirements Traceability Matrix.
  4. Define product and project scope boundaries.
  5. Decompose approved scope into the WBS and WBS dictionary within the Scope Baseline.
  6. Deliver and control scope while preserving traceability.
  7. Verify completed deliverables before seeking formal acceptance.

docs.title: Handoffs
docs.text:
What enters

Charter, stakeholder needs, product information, assumptions, constraints, standards, risk, and delivery approach.

What this work accomplishes

Defines what must be satisfied, what work is authorized, and what evidence will demonstrate completion.

What moves next

Approved scope drives schedule, cost, quality, resources, procurement, delivery, verification, acceptance, and change control.

docs.title: Feedback and rejection loops
docs.text: Unclear or conflicting requirements return to stakeholders for analysis. Decomposition can reveal missing scope or infeasible assumptions. During delivery, requested scope changes enter integrated change control. A deliverable that fails inspection returns for defect analysis and authorized rework; a verified deliverable that is not accepted returns for clarification, correction, change evaluation, or another authorized disposition.

docs.title: Roles, authority, and approaches
docs.text:
Stakeholders supply needs and acceptance expectations. The project team analyzes and decomposes the work. The project manager coordinates control. An authorized customer, sponsor, product owner, or other designated role makes the applicable acceptance decision; verification by the quality function is not that formal acceptance.

Predictive work may baseline a broad scope structure. Adaptive work refines prioritized items and acceptance criteria over short horizons while preserving outcome and traceability. Hybrid work must map evolving items to controlled commitments and approval boundaries.

docs.title: Artifact states and exam distinctions
docs.text:
A need becomes a documented requirement, a requirement becomes traceable to approved scope and delivery work, a completed deliverable becomes verified through quality control, and a verified deliverable becomes accepted only through an authorized acceptance decision. The WBS organizes scope; it is not a schedule or organizational chart.

docs.title: Risk, Compliance, and Procurement
docs.text:
Lifecycle chapter 6

Risk, Compliance, and Procurement

Uncertainty, mandatory obligations, and external commitments affect one another and must remain visible from planning through closure.

Lifecycle orientation

docs.title: Process Phases
docs.text:
These process groups overlap and repeat; the emphasis shows where this chapter most often concentrates.

  1. InitiatingProcess group
  2. PlanningProcess group · emphasized
  3. ExecutingProcess group · emphasized
  4. Monitoring and ControllingProcess group · emphasized
  5. ClosingProcess group · emphasized

docs.title: Local sequence
docs.text:
1. Plan the risk approach, identify uncertainties, and build the Risk Register.
  2. Prioritize risks and perform quantitative analysis when warranted and supported.
  3. Select responses, assign owners, implement agreed actions, and monitor residual and emerging risk.
  4. Trace compliance obligations into requirements, scope, quality criteria, risk, procurement terms, acceptance evidence, and closure records.
  5. Plan procurement, prepare solicitation information, select sellers through authorized conduct, and establish agreements.
  6. Control seller performance, changes, claims, records, and completion; close contractual obligations through the applicable authority.

docs.title: Handoffs
docs.text:
What enters

Objectives, scope, assumptions, constraints, compliance obligations, market information, risk appetite, and make-or-buy considerations.

What this work accomplishes

Makes uncertainty actionable, obligations traceable, and external commitments governable.

What moves next

Responses, owners, procurement decisions, agreements, controls, and evidence enter execution, monitoring, acceptance, and closure.

docs.title: Feedback, issues, and authority
docs.text:
A risk trigger can create response work, an issue, or a change request. A compliance finding can block acceptance or require corrective action. Seller performance can change schedule, cost, quality, and risk. These paths return through domain control and integrated change rather than bypassing authority.

Risk owners monitor assigned uncertainties; response owners perform agreed actions. Procurement authority depends on organizational policy and agreement terms. Compliance authority depends on the governing obligation. The project manager integrates impacts but does not invent authority beyond the project governance model.

docs.title: Approach treatment and exam distinctions
docs.text:
Predictive work may establish broader risk and procurement structures early. Adaptive work reviews uncertainty and obligations frequently as increments evolve. Hybrid work must connect adaptive discovery to contract, baseline, and compliance controls.

A risk is uncertain; an issue has occurred. A contingency response differs from an unapproved scope change. Contract type influences risk allocation but does not eliminate buyer oversight. Compliance is not a closing checklist: it must be traceable from requirements through evidence and handoff. Detailed contract and audit claims remain in the process references or deferred until current primary sources support them.

docs.title: Schedule, Resources, and Cost
docs.text:
Lifecycle chapter 4

Schedule, Resources, and Cost

Time, people, equipment, and funding form one constraint system; planning or controlling them independently produces an infeasible project.

Lifecycle orientation

docs.title: Process Phases
docs.text:
These process groups overlap and repeat; the emphasis shows where this chapter most often concentrates.

  1. InitiatingProcess group
  2. PlanningProcess group · emphasized
  3. ExecutingProcess group · emphasized
  4. Monitoring and ControllingProcess group · emphasized
  5. ClosingProcess group

docs.title: Local sequence
docs.text:
1. Translate scope components into activities and milestones.
  2. Establish logical relationships and identify resource needs.
  3. Estimate durations and costs with explicit assumptions.
  4. Analyze constraints and integrate the current Project Schedule.
  5. Aggregate estimates, reconcile funding, and approve the Schedule Baseline and Cost Baseline.
  6. Acquire and coordinate resources while execution produces actuals.
  7. Compare actual and forecast conditions with authorized baselines; decide recovery, escalation, or change.

docs.title: Handoffs
docs.text:
What enters

Scope baseline, calendars, resource information, rates, constraints, risk, procurement lead times, and estimating evidence.

What this work accomplishes

Creates a feasible coordination model and authorized comparison points for time and cost.

What moves next

Schedules, assignments, estimates, and baselines guide execution; actuals and forecasts return to monitoring and decisions.

docs.title: Feedback and authority
docs.text:
Unavailable resources can force new sequencing or duration assumptions. Schedule compression can affect cost, quality, and risk. Funding limits can force scope or timing decisions. Performance variance returns through control processes; corrective action may adjust work within authority, while a baseline-affecting proposal enters integrated change control.

The project manager integrates tradeoffs. Activity owners and specialists contribute estimates. Resource managers or functional leaders commit controlled resources. Sponsors or governance bodies decide changes beyond delegated thresholds.

docs.title: Approach treatment and artifact states
docs.text:
Predictive work often models a broader activity network and baselines. Adaptive work plans near-term items and capacity in more detail, using cadence and flow evidence to forecast. Hybrid work maps iteration or flow commitments to external milestones and funding controls.

The current schedule and forecasts are working information. Baselines are approved comparison records. Variance is not permission to rewrite them. Formulas remain canonically explained in relevant process material until repository sources support a shared formula registry.

docs.title: Exam distinctions
docs.text:
Duration is elapsed working time, not effort. Estimates are not authorized budgets. A forecast is not a baseline. Resource leveling, schedule compression, reserve decisions, and earned-value interpretations must be evaluated for downstream risk and authority, not applied as isolated calculations.

docs.title: Delivery approach applicability
docs.text:
→Predictive⇄Hybrid Predictive treatmentPerformed as the formally named process, often using approved plans, baselines, decision rights, or formal controls. Adaptive equivalent or treatmentAdaptive delivery addresses the underlying purpose through product, team, or flow practices, but not necessarily through this formally named process. Hybrid treatmentCommonly provides governance, funding, contractual, compliance, milestone, or integration control around adaptive delivery. Why these badgesThe registered hybrid source explicitly describes adaptive product delivery operating within predictive governance and fixed constraints.

Source-limited crosswalk: Predictive classification is supported by the canonical process catalog. Cross-approach treatments are an Atlas synthesis of the registered 2026 course snapshot and are not a PMI process-to-agile-framework crosswalk.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Obtain the people, facilities, equipment, materials, and other resources needed to perform authorized project work.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: A plan that assumes resources are available does not make them available. Acquisition reconciles project needs with organizational priorities, supplier capacity, timing, and actual assignments. Delayed or unsuitable resources can invalidate schedule, cost, and quality assumptions.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Resource estimates and the resource-management approach define the need, while procurement and organizational processes may help fulfill it. Confirmed assignments and physical resources enable execution, team development, and ongoing management; shortfalls may require replanning or escalation. Acquisition can recur as work packages start or resource needs change.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Acquire Resources secures team and physical resources. Develop Team improves team capability and cohesion after people are assigned, while Manage Team addresses ongoing performance and issues. Estimating a need is not acquiring it.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

An airport baggage-system upgrade needs controls engineers, overnight installation crews, test equipment, and temporary storage. The project manager negotiates internal assignments and contracts specialized equipment for the required windows. The confirmed resources allow detailed work to begin and the newly formed team to develop operating routines.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Look for negotiation, assignment, or obtaining resources—not training or resolving team performance.
  2. The project manager may need functional managers, procurement staff, or sellers to secure resources.
  3. If acquisition differs from the plan, assess schedule, cost, and risk effects rather than silently assuming the gap away.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Confirm that the project or phase is formally complete, transition its results, resolve remaining administrative obligations, and preserve useful records and learning.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Finishing the last activity does not prove that obligations, acceptance, transition, contracts, records, and organizational learning have been addressed. Formal closure establishes a defensible end state and releases attention and resources deliberately. Skipping it leaves unresolved ownership, open commitments, and weak evidence of completion.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Closure depends on completion information, acceptance where applicable, and resolution of outstanding work. It consolidates final records and lessons, transitions the result, and closes the authorized project or phase; procurement closure may also occur as contracts reach completion. A terminated project still requires an orderly close.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Close Project or Phase is a management process, not the moment the final scheduled activity ends. Deliverable acceptance may occur earlier through Validate Scope, and individual contracts may be closed through Control Procurements while the wider project continues.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

After a university opens a new research laboratory, the team confirms acceptance, transfers operating procedures to facilities staff, closes remaining supplier obligations, archives approvals, and documents commissioning lessons. Only then does the sponsor formally close the project and release the remaining project resources.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Look for formal completion, transition, records, and lessons—not merely completed production work.
  2. Premature termination changes the reason for closing, not the need to close responsibly.
  3. Accepted deliverables support closure, but acceptance and project closure are distinct decisions.

docs.title: Delivery approach applicability
docs.text:
→Predictive↻Adaptive⇄Hybrid Predictive treatmentEstablishes the relevant plan or definition with greater upfront detail and controlled updates. Adaptive equivalent or treatmentThe management purpose is handled iteratively through vision, roadmap, backlog refinement, iteration or release planning, feedback, and progressive elaboration. Hybrid treatmentAdaptive planning cadence is coordinated with predictive milestones, funding, compliance, contracts, or approved control points. Why these badgesThe registered adaptive source explicitly supports iterative planning, refinement, forecasting, feedback, and hybrid governance overlays.

Source-limited crosswalk: Predictive classification is supported by the canonical process catalog. Cross-approach treatments are an Atlas synthesis of the registered 2026 course snapshot and are not a PMI process-to-agile-framework crosswalk.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Elicit, analyze, and document stakeholder needs and conditions so later scope, design, verification, and acceptance decisions have a traceable basis.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: A solution can satisfy its stated scope and still fail if the underlying needs were incomplete, ambiguous, or attributed to the wrong stakeholders. Requirements work makes expectations examinable and exposes conflicts early. Traceability helps the team understand why each requirement exists and how it will be checked.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Stakeholder identification and the planned scope approach establish whom to involve and how to work. The resulting requirements inform Define Scope, quality planning, solution work, and eventual verification and acceptance; they may be refined as understanding grows. Collection explores needs—it does not yet settle the complete project boundary.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Collect Requirements captures and analyzes needs. Define Scope decides which requirements and constraints are included in the detailed boundary, while Validate Scope later seeks formal acceptance of completed deliverables.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A clinic is redesigning patient intake. Interviews and observation reveal needs from patients, nurses, privacy staff, interpreters, and billing specialists, including accessibility and data-handling conditions. The team traces those needs into the proposed service scope and later test and acceptance criteria.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. If stakeholders are expressing needs or resolving requirement ambiguity, the work precedes detailed scope definition.
  2. A requested feature is not automatically approved project scope; it must be evaluated with other needs and constraints.
  3. Traceability connects a requirement to its origin and downstream verification, reducing orphan requirements.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Obtain and evaluate seller responses, select an appropriate seller, negotiate as authorized, and establish an agreement for external work.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: A sourcing strategy becomes useful only when the project applies it fairly and selects a seller whose offer can satisfy the need. This process turns market responses into a governed commercial commitment. Weak evaluation can trade a low initial price for unacceptable risk, capability, or contract ambiguity.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Procurement documents, evaluation criteria, seller responses, and organizational authority shape the selection. The resulting agreement and seller relationship enable externally supplied work and become the basis for Control Procurements. Additional procurements may be conducted as later needs are authorized.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Conduct Procurements selects and contracts with a seller. Plan Procurement Management defines the sourcing approach, while Control Procurements monitors agreement performance, changes, claims, and closure after award.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A transit agency evaluates proposals for fare-payment equipment using technical compliance, implementation approach, support capacity, delivery risk, and total commercial terms. After clarification and authorized negotiation, it selects a seller and executes an agreement. The project team then controls performance against that agreement.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Seller selection should follow the approved evaluation approach rather than an improvised preference.
  2. Contract authority and procurement rules matter; the project manager may participate without having sole authority to bind the organization.
  3. After award, performance issues belong in Control Procurements rather than repeating source selection.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Analyze cost performance and forecasts, influence the factors causing variance, and manage changes to the approved cost baseline.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Recording invoices does not explain whether the project is receiving the expected progress for its spending or where final cost is heading. Cost control connects actual performance, remaining work, and forecasts so management can act. It protects financial commitments while allowing justified change through governance.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Execution supplies cost and progress information that is compared with the baseline established during budgeting. Analysis may produce updated forecasts, corrective actions, or change requests, and its conclusions contribute to overall project monitoring. The process repeats as new performance evidence becomes available.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Control Costs evaluates cost performance against the baseline and forecasts outcomes. Determine Budget creates the authorized baseline, while Monitor and Control Project Work integrates cost findings with other project dimensions.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A housing retrofit program has spent less than planned, but completed units are also below plan because specialist crews are unavailable. Cost control analyzes the relationship between spending and progress, updates the completion forecast, and recommends a staffing response rather than treating the apparent underspend as good performance.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Cost status requires context about accomplished work; lower spending alone is not necessarily favorable.
  2. Forecast updates do not automatically change the approved cost baseline.
  3. A baseline-changing response follows the project’s change-control authority.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Manage seller and buyer performance against agreements, administer changes and claims, maintain appropriate records, and close contractual relationships.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Signing an agreement does not ensure that external work will meet project needs. Contract control connects technical progress with commercial obligations and provides a governed way to address variance, change, disputes, payment, and completion. Neglect creates both delivery and legal exposure.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Agreements, performance evidence, inspections, invoices, and correspondence provide the control basis. Findings may lead to corrective action, contractual change, claims handling, or broader project change control; completed obligations support contract closure and eventually project closure. Oversight continues for each active procurement.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Control Procurements manages the contractual relationship and agreement performance. Control Quality verifies technical conformance of results, and Close Project or Phase closes the wider project or phase. Contract closure can occur before project closure.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A software vendor is meeting feature requirements but missing agreed response times and documentation dates. The buyer reviews evidence against the agreement, issues the required notice, agrees on a recovery action, and processes an authorized contractual change. Final completion is documented when all obligations are satisfied.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Use the agreement as the governing reference for seller obligations and buyer remedies.
  2. Technical acceptance, payment authorization, contract closure, and project closure are related but distinct decisions.
  3. A contract change may also require integrated project change control when project baselines are affected.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Inspect, measure, and record results to determine whether deliverables and performance conform to defined quality requirements.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: A completed item is not ready for acceptance merely because the team believes it is finished. Objective checks provide evidence of conformance and identify defects or corrective needs before stakeholder acceptance. Without verification, nonconforming work can move downstream and become more expensive to correct.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Quality metrics and completed work provide the basis for inspection and measurement. Conforming results become verified deliverables that can proceed to Validate Scope; defects may lead to rework, process improvement, or change requests. Control Quality repeats as deliverables are produced.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Manage Quality evaluates and improves the processes used to create results. Control Quality checks the results themselves. Validate Scope then obtains formal acceptance of verified deliverables from the authorized stakeholder.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

Before a new warehouse conveyor is presented to operations, the team tests throughput, safety interlocks, stopping distance, and error handling against the agreed criteria. Failed tests trigger correction and retesting. The passing system becomes a verified deliverable for the operations sponsor’s acceptance review.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Verification answers whether specified criteria were met; acceptance answers whether the authorized stakeholder accepts the result.
  2. A defect found during inspection belongs in Control Quality even if its cause later drives Manage Quality improvement.
  3. Follow the deliverable state: completed, verified, and accepted are not interchangeable.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Confirm that physical resources are available and used as planned, identify variances, and take action when equipment, materials, or facilities do not match project needs.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Even acquired resources can be unavailable, consumed faster than expected, misallocated, or released at the wrong time. Physical-resource control protects work continuity and cost and schedule assumptions. It creates active visibility rather than relying on inventory or allocation plans that may no longer be current.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Resource plans, assignments, usage information, and execution needs provide the comparison basis. Variances may lead to reallocation, replenishment, corrective action, or change requests and inform overall monitoring. Control continues while physical resources are required.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Control Resources concerns physical resources such as equipment, materials, and facilities. Manage Team addresses people’s performance and relationships. Acquire Resources obtains resources; control checks their continuing availability and use.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A road project discovers that aggregate is being consumed faster than planned and a shared compactor has been reassigned. The team reconciles usage, secures a replacement equipment window, and adjusts deliveries before paving stops. Cost and schedule forecasts are updated with the resulting effects.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Use Control Resources for physical availability and utilization, not personnel coaching.
  2. Acquisition success does not eliminate the need to monitor consumption, condition, allocation, and release.
  3. A material or equipment variance may require corrective action without automatically changing a baseline.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Assess schedule performance, forecast timing outcomes, and manage changes to the approved schedule baseline.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: A published schedule becomes obsolete unless actual progress and emerging constraints are analyzed. Schedule control distinguishes ordinary forecast movement from variance that requires action or formal change. It helps the team respond before missed dates cascade across dependent work.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Execution supplies progress and current forecasts, which are compared with the schedule model and baseline. Analysis may lead to corrective action, resequencing, updated forecasts, or change requests; approved baseline changes are incorporated through governance. Control recurs throughout the work rather than waiting for a missed milestone.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Control Schedule analyzes timing performance and manages the schedule baseline. Monitor and Control Project Work integrates schedule findings with the project’s overall health, and Perform Integrated Change Control decides controlled change requests.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A public-health campaign finds that translation approvals are running two weeks late. The scheduler updates actual progress, analyzes downstream printing and distribution effects, and tests recovery options. The team resequences unaffected work and submits a baseline change only where the authorized completion commitment must move.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Updating a forecast is not necessarily the same as changing the approved schedule baseline.
  2. Use dependency logic to assess the effect of delay rather than treating every late activity as equally important.
  3. Corrective action can be proposed in schedule control but may require integrated approval before implementation.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Monitor the status of project and product scope and manage proposed or actual changes to the approved scope baseline.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Scope can drift through informal requests, misunderstood requirements, or work that no longer matches approved boundaries. Active control detects variance, assesses its cause and impact, and routes necessary changes through the established process. It protects the baseline without assuming that all change is undesirable.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Actual work and completed deliverables are compared with approved scope information. Variances or stakeholder requests may lead to corrective action or change requests, while approved changes update the relevant baseline and plans. Control occurs throughout delivery and uses requirement traceability and acceptance information where relevant.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Validate Scope asks whether an authorized stakeholder accepts a completed deliverable. Control Scope asks whether current work and boundaries remain aligned with the approved scope baseline and manages changes to that baseline.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

During a retail-store rollout, local managers ask each site team to add custom signage not included in the approved package. The project manager identifies the cumulative scope impact, stops informal additions, and submits a consolidated change for cost, schedule, and brand review. Approved variants are then incorporated into the baseline.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Scope control does not mean refusing every change; it means preventing uncontrolled change.
  2. A rejected deliverable may trigger corrective work, while a requested boundary change may require integrated change control.
  3. Acceptance status and baseline status answer different questions.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Decompose the approved project scope into manageable components that provide a structured basis for planning, responsibility, estimating, and control.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Large deliverables are too broad to estimate, assign, or monitor reliably. Decomposition creates a complete, organized view of the authorized scope at a level the project can manage. Poor decomposition hides work, duplicates responsibility, or encourages teams to schedule activities before understanding the deliverables.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: The detailed scope description and requirements establish what must be represented. The WBS organizes that scope into progressively smaller components and supports activity definition, estimates, budgeting, responsibility decisions, and scope control. Decomposition can be elaborated as information becomes available, while the approved scope baseline remains controlled.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Create WBS decomposes deliverables and project scope into manageable components. Define Activities later identifies the actions needed to produce those components. A WBS is not a chronological task list or organization chart.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A utility is replacing a water-treatment control system. The team decomposes the project into design, equipment, site preparation, installation, migration, testing, training, and transition components, then breaks each to a manageable level. Schedule planners use those components to define activities without losing sight of the complete authorized scope.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Think deliverable-oriented decomposition before activity sequencing.
  2. The WBS should represent the full authorized scope; omitted work will distort estimates and control.
  3. More detail is not automatically better—the useful level is one the project can estimate, assign, and monitor.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Identify the specific schedule activities needed to produce the project’s planned work packages and deliverables.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: A WBS shows what scope must be delivered but may not expose the actions needed to create it. Defining activities translates manageable scope components into work that can be ordered, estimated, assigned, and tracked. Missing activities create false confidence in dates and resource needs.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: The scope baseline and scheduling approach provide the structure for identifying work. The activity list then supports dependency sequencing, duration and resource estimates, and schedule development. Activities can be elaborated as near-term work becomes clearer, especially in rolling-wave planning.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Create WBS decomposes scope into deliverable-oriented components. Define Activities identifies the actions needed to produce those components. Sequence Activities then determines their logical relationships.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

For a pharmaceutical packaging-line upgrade, the WBS includes a validated labeling station. The team defines activities for design approval, equipment preparation, installation, software configuration, protocol execution, training, and release. Those activities can then be sequenced and estimated.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. If the work is being translated from work packages into schedulable actions, this is activity definition.
  2. Do not confuse identifying an activity with deciding its order or duration.
  3. Progressive elaboration can add detail without implying that the original scope was uncontrolled.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Develop a detailed description of the project and product boundaries by selecting and clarifying the work and results the project will include.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: A requirements set can contain competing wishes, optional features, and unresolved boundaries. Scope definition turns that information into a coherent statement of what the project will deliver and what lies outside its responsibility. Weak boundaries create expectation gaps and uncontrolled expansion.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Defined requirements, assumptions, constraints, and planning decisions provide the basis for the detailed scope. The result supports decomposition in Create WBS, schedule and cost planning, quality criteria, and later scope validation and control. It may be refined iteratively as product understanding improves through approved decisions.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Collect Requirements identifies and analyzes needs; Define Scope chooses and describes the included boundary; Create WBS decomposes that approved boundary into manageable components. Definition is not decomposition.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A museum plans a traveling exhibition. Requirements include multilingual interpretation, educational programming, insurance, and possible augmented reality. The team defines the funded exhibition boundary, explicitly excludes a permanent gallery renovation, and passes the approved scope description into WBS development and estimating.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Look for decisions about what is included and excluded, not merely a list of stakeholder requests.
  2. The detailed scope description precedes decomposition into the WBS.
  3. Refining scope is legitimate; changing an approved baseline later requires appropriate control.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Aggregate project cost estimates into an authorized, time-aware cost baseline and establish the funding view needed to support the work.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: A collection of estimates does not show when money is needed, what performance will be measured against, or whether the project is financially authorized. Budget determination reconciles estimates with schedule, funding constraints, and governance. Without it, spending decisions lack a coherent baseline.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Cost estimates and schedule timing are consolidated, reviewed, and aligned with funding limits. The approved cost baseline supports Control Costs and overall performance reporting; later baseline changes require appropriate authorization. Budget development may iterate when estimates, timing, or funding constraints cannot be reconciled.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Estimate Costs asks what individual work is expected to cost. Determine Budget aggregates and authorizes the baseline and funding profile used to measure cost performance. A total estimate is not automatically an approved cost baseline.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A food manufacturer combines equipment, construction, commissioning, training, and contingency estimates for a new production line. Mapping those costs to the schedule reveals a funding peak during installation, so finance and the sponsor adjust the release plan before approving the baseline. Control Costs later measures performance against it.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Look for aggregation, authorization, funding timing, or establishment of the cost baseline.
  2. The cost baseline is a performance reference; actual expenditures and forecasts are compared with it later.
  3. If funding constraints force schedule or scope tradeoffs, planning may iterate before authorization.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Establish that a proposed project or phase is worth undertaking, authorize it to proceed, and give the project manager authority to coordinate the work.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: A promising idea is not yet an authorized project. The charter connects the intended outcome to an organizational need and establishes enough authority and shared direction to justify detailed planning. Without that foundation, teams may spend money or make commitments without a recognized sponsor, objective, or decision boundary.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Authorization draws on the business reason for the work and the sponsor’s expectations. Once the charter exists, stakeholders can be identified more deliberately and the integrated project management plan can be developed within an approved mandate. A charter may be revisited when a phase is authorized, but it is not the detailed plan for performing the work.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Develop Project Charter authorizes and frames the project or phase; Develop Project Management Plan integrates the detailed approach for executing, monitoring, and closing it. Approval to investigate or begin is not the same as approval of every later baseline or delivery decision.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A hospital proposes replacing its medication-dispensing system after repeated delay incidents. The sponsor confirms the safety objective, expected operational benefit, initial boundaries, and project manager authority in the charter. Department leaders then use that authorization to identify affected clinical stakeholders and begin integrated planning.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. When a scenario lacks formal authority or sponsor alignment, look to the charter before detailed planning.
  2. A charter is high-level authorization; it does not substitute for the project management plan or its subsidiary components.
  3. The project manager may help develop the charter, but authorization comes from an appropriate sponsor or initiating authority.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Combine the project’s planning decisions into a coordinated basis for directing work, measuring performance, controlling change, and closing the effort.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Separate scope, schedule, cost, quality, resource, and risk decisions can conflict even when each looks reasonable alone. Integration exposes those conflicts and establishes how the parts will work together. Without an integrated plan, teams optimize locally and lack a common basis for execution or control.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: The charter supplies authority and high-level direction; subsidiary planning and baselines contribute progressively more detail. The resulting plan guides Direct and Manage Project Work and provides the reference used by monitoring and integrated change control. It is progressively elaborated and updated through controlled decisions rather than frozen after one planning event.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: The project charter explains why the project is authorized and establishes high-level direction. The project management plan explains how the authorized work will be executed and controlled by integrating approved planning components. Neither is simply a schedule.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A manufacturer is preparing a new product launch. Marketing’s release date, engineering’s validation work, procurement lead times, quality reviews, and budget constraints are reconciled into one governing plan. Delivery teams use that integrated basis to coordinate work, while proposed baseline changes are evaluated across all affected areas.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Choose this process when the issue is coordination among planning components, not creation of one specialized plan.
  2. Approved baselines and subsidiary plans are components of the integrated plan; they are not unrelated documents.
  3. An approved change is incorporated through controlled updates, not by informally rewriting the plan.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Integrate activity logic, duration and resource estimates, calendars, constraints, and project objectives into an analyzed schedule model and usable timing commitments.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Individual estimates do not reveal the combined feasibility of the project. Schedule development exposes critical relationships, resource conflicts, limited flexibility, and tradeoffs before dates are approved. Without integrated analysis, milestones may be politically attractive but operationally impossible.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Activities, dependencies, durations, resource information, and constraints converge here. The resulting schedule guides execution and becomes the reference for Control Schedule; iteration may send the team back to refine estimates, logic, or resource choices. Approved changes and actual performance later update the model through control.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Sequence Activities creates dependency logic and Estimate Activity Durations supplies time estimates. Develop Schedule combines those inputs with resources and constraints to calculate and optimize the overall model.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A renewable-energy developer integrates permitting, equipment fabrication, site work, grid interconnection, testing, and seasonal access constraints. Analysis reveals that transformer delivery governs the target energization date, so the team adjusts procurement timing and parallel site work before approving the schedule.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Choose Develop Schedule when separate scheduling inputs are being integrated into dates and a feasible model.
  2. A schedule forecast can change with actual performance without every change becoming an unauthorized baseline change.
  3. Compression or resource adjustment should be evaluated for effects on cost, risk, and quality.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Improve team members’ capabilities, working relationships, and environment so the project team can perform effectively together.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Assembling skilled individuals does not automatically create a capable project team. Shared practices, trust, feedback, learning, and a workable environment reduce coordination loss and improve collective performance. Development is especially important when the team is new, distributed, or working across organizational boundaries.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Acquired team members and the resource-management approach establish the starting conditions. Development activities strengthen capability during execution and can respond to observations from Manage Team; learning also supports project knowledge. Team development continues as membership and challenges change.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Develop Team builds capability and cohesion. Manage Team tracks performance, gives feedback, resolves conflict, and coordinates changes for specific performance needs. Acquire Resources obtains the people in the first place.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A distributed product-launch team has marketing, regulatory, engineering, and regional sales members who have never worked together. They establish shared decision routines, practice handoffs through a launch simulation, and pair regional staff with subject experts. Later performance issues are handled through Manage Team.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Training, team-building, recognition, and improved working conditions point toward team development.
  2. Conflict can reveal a development need, but handling a specific performance issue is often Manage Team.
  3. Team development is iterative; it does not end after a kickoff workshop.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Lead and perform the authorized work, produce project results, and implement approved changes in accordance with the project management plan.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Planning has value only when coordinated action turns it into deliverables and usable work results. This process aligns people, resources, and approved decisions during delivery. Without it, execution becomes a collection of disconnected tasks and unauthorized adjustments.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: The project management plan supplies the governing direction, while approved changes may alter what the team performs. Work results and performance information feed quality, knowledge, monitoring, and change-control activities. Execution and control interact continuously; discovering a variance does not itself authorize the team to change a baseline.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Direct and Manage Project Work performs authorized work and approved changes. Monitor and Control Project Work evaluates overall performance, while Perform Integrated Change Control decides what to do with change requests. Approval and implementation are separate decisions.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

During an office relocation, the team coordinates furniture installation, network cutover, staff communications, and approved floor-plan changes. Progress and issues are reported for monitoring, and only approved changes are incorporated into the work. The result is a functioning workplace ready for operational handoff.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. If the scenario says an approved change now needs to be carried out, this is the integration process that implements it.
  2. Work performance data originates from doing the work; analysis of overall performance belongs in monitoring.
  3. Do not treat execution as permission to bypass change control when a baseline would be affected.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Estimate the working time each schedule activity will require under the expected resource, productivity, calendar, and uncertainty conditions.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Dates built from unsupported guesses cannot support commitments or meaningful forecasts. Duration estimation makes assumptions visible and relates the amount of work to the way it will be performed. Ignoring resource capability, availability, or uncertainty produces schedules that fail under ordinary conditions.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Defined and sequenced activities, resource expectations, and relevant experience inform the estimates. The durations are combined with network logic and constraints in Develop Schedule and are refined as knowledge or execution evidence improves. A duration estimate is elapsed working time, not automatically the effort hours or final calendar dates.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Estimate Activity Durations estimates how long an activity takes with expected resources. Estimate Activity Resources determines the types and quantities of resources needed, while Develop Schedule calculates dates for the connected work.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A laboratory automation project estimates configuration, validation, and training durations using vendor experience, staff availability, test-volume assumptions, and uncertainty around regulatory review. Schedule development then combines those estimates with dependencies and calendars to forecast the go-live date.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Separate duration from effort: adding people does not always reduce elapsed time proportionally.
  2. Estimates should reflect expected resources and calendars, not an unconstrained ideal.
  3. Refinement is normal when better information becomes available; it is not evidence that planning occurred only once.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Estimate the types and quantities of team members, materials, equipment, facilities, and other resources needed for each activity.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Duration and cost estimates are unreliable when resource assumptions remain implicit. This process tests whether planned activities can be staffed and supplied in a realistic way and exposes scarcity, capability, or availability concerns. It creates a basis for acquisition and schedule analysis without promising that every resource is already secured.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Defined activities, work requirements, organizational capacity, and the resource-management approach shape the estimates. The results inform duration and cost estimates, schedule development, procurement decisions, and Acquire Resources; they are refined as designs and availability become clearer.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Estimate Activity Resources determines what and how much an activity needs. Estimate Activity Durations estimates elapsed working time with expected resources, and Acquire Resources obtains the selected people and physical resources.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

For a stadium event, planners estimate security staff by entrance and shift, medical teams by attendance profile, generators by electrical load, and barriers by crowd-flow design. Those quantities feed vendor sourcing, staffing assignments, duration planning, and the event budget.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. An estimate of resource type or quantity is not an acquisition commitment.
  2. Resource assumptions affect both duration and cost, so those planning activities often iterate.
  3. Distinguish a capability requirement from a named assignment; acquisition happens later.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Develop reasoned estimates of the monetary resources needed to complete project activities and work.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Funding and tradeoff decisions require more than a single optimistic total. Cost estimation makes the basis, uncertainty, and components of expected spending visible. Weak estimates obscure risk and make later budget performance difficult to interpret.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Scope, schedule, resource, procurement, and risk information provide the estimating basis. Individual estimates are aggregated and reconciled during Determine Budget and are refined as design or market information improves. Estimating predicts likely cost; it does not itself authorize the total budget.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Estimate Costs develops costs for activities or work components. Determine Budget aggregates those estimates, accounts for timing and authorized reserves as appropriate, and establishes the approved cost baseline and funding requirements.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A municipal bridge-repair team estimates engineering, traffic control, labor, materials, equipment, environmental monitoring, and specialist subcontract costs using current quantities and market information. The estimates include stated uncertainty and are later aggregated into the funding and cost-baseline decision.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. An estimate supports a decision; it is not the same as an approved budget.
  2. Look for the basis and uncertainty of component costs before aggregation.
  3. Changes in scope, schedule, resources, or risk can require estimates to be revisited.
