docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Discover and describe uncertain events or conditions that could affect objectives, including both threats and opportunities.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: A project can manage only the uncertainties it recognizes or remains prepared to discover. Broad identification draws on diverse perspectives and exposes causes, events, and possible effects before they become issues. Treating the first list as complete leaves the project blind to emerging risk.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: The planned risk approach and current scope, schedule, cost, procurement, stakeholder, and technical information guide the search. Identified risks move into qualitative analysis and, when warranted, quantitative analysis and response planning; identification continues throughout the project.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Identify Risks discovers and describes uncertainty. Perform Qualitative Risk Analysis prioritizes identified risks, while an issue is a condition that has already occurred and needs present action.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

Before a vaccine-storage expansion, the team identifies possible permit delay, refrigeration supply shortage, power instability, staff availability, and an opportunity to combine purchasing with another program. The risks are described with potential causes and effects, then prioritized for analysis.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Include opportunities as well as threats.
  2. Do not jump from a newly identified risk directly to an arbitrary response before assessing significance.
  3. Identification is iterative; execution, changes, and monitoring can reveal new risks.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Determine who can affect the project, who may be affected by it, and what is initially known about their interests, influence, and involvement.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Plans fail when important voices, decision rights, or sources of resistance remain invisible. Early stakeholder analysis lets the team recognize whose support, expertise, approval, or adaptation will matter. Missing a stakeholder can produce late requirements, blocked decisions, or avoidable opposition.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: The charter and emerging project context provide an initial boundary for the search. The results inform requirements work, communications planning, risk identification, and stakeholder engagement planning. Identification continues throughout the project because roles, influence, and affected groups can change.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Identify Stakeholders establishes who matters and why; Plan Stakeholder Engagement selects an approach for involving them; Manage Stakeholder Engagement carries out that approach. A contact list alone is not stakeholder analysis.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A city begins a downtown bus-lane project. The team identifies transit riders, nearby businesses, emergency services, accessibility advocates, road-maintenance staff, and permitting authorities, then records their differing influence and concerns. That analysis shapes later workshops, traffic studies, and engagement plans.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Identification is not confined to Initiating; newly affected or newly influential stakeholders should be added when discovered.
  2. Separate finding and analyzing stakeholders from communicating with or actively engaging them.
  3. In situational questions, an unexpected influential party usually calls for analysis before choosing a response.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Carry out agreed risk-response actions so planned treatment changes the project’s actual exposure.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Risk registers often contain well-designed actions that never occur because they lack follow-through, timing, or coordination. Implementation closes the gap between intention and action. It makes ownership observable and integrates responses with the work rather than treating risk management as a reporting exercise.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Approved response plans and assigned owners establish what should be performed. Execution evidence then feeds Monitor Risks, which evaluates whether the action occurred and whether it changed exposure; ineffective responses may require adjustment or new planning. Implementation happens when the planned trigger or timing requires it.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Plan Risk Responses selects and integrates the action. Implement Risk Responses performs it. Monitor Risks checks exposure, triggers, and effectiveness. Marking an action 'planned' is not evidence that it was carried out.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A conference team planned a backup venue contract if wildfire conditions crossed an agreed trigger. When the threshold is reached, the response owner activates the reservation, redirects logistics, and updates attendee communication. Monitoring then tracks air quality and the operational effects of the move.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Look for execution of an already agreed response, not selection of a strategy.
  2. Risk owners support accountability, but response actions must still be coordinated with authorized project work.
  3. After implementation, monitor whether exposure changed as intended and whether new risks appeared.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Create, distribute, retrieve, and manage project information so stakeholders receive usable information through the planned channels and at the needed time.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Information only supports decisions when it reaches the right audience in a form they can understand and use. This process turns the communications approach into day-to-day information flow and responds to immediate communication needs. It also protects consistency, confidentiality, and accessibility where required.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: The communications plan and current project information guide production and distribution. Stakeholder responses and observed information needs feed Monitor Communications and may lead to adjustments in content or channels. Communication occurs continuously alongside execution and stakeholder engagement.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Manage Communications performs the communication work. Monitor Communications assesses whether communication is effective and whether needs are being met. Manage Stakeholder Engagement uses interaction to address expectations and involvement, not merely transmit information.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

During an enterprise policy rollout, the project team publishes role-specific guidance, gives managers briefing packs, maintains a controlled question log, and issues urgent corrections through an agreed channel. Feedback shows where messages are misunderstood, giving Monitor Communications evidence for changes.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Producing and distributing information points to Manage Communications; evaluating its effectiveness points to Monitor Communications.
  2. Communication is two-way when understanding or feedback matters; transmission alone may be insufficient.
  3. Tailor content without creating conflicting versions of the project’s current information.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Apply relevant existing knowledge to project decisions and capture new learning so it can improve current and future work.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Teams repeatedly lose time when experience remains with individuals or lessons are recorded only after they can no longer help. Deliberate knowledge management makes expertise usable and creates feedback while work is still underway. It also reduces dependence on a few people and preserves learning beyond the project.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Knowledge is drawn from organizational experience, specialists, and current project activity. It supports execution, problem solving, quality improvement, risk responses, and later planning updates; new learning is shared back into the project and organization. The process is continuous and social, not merely a closing documentation exercise.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Manage Project Knowledge is broader than maintaining a lessons-learned record. A repository can store explicit information, but transferring tacit experience may require conversation, observation, mentoring, or collaborative review.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A construction team encounters unexpected soil conditions similar to those on an earlier site. A geotechnical specialist from the prior project reviews the response with the current team, which adapts the excavation approach and records the reasoning. The lesson helps current risk and schedule decisions and becomes available to future projects.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Look for both using existing knowledge and creating new knowledge; the process is not limited to archiving lessons.
  2. A lesson can be useful during execution, so do not wait for Close Project or Phase to capture and share it.
  3. Tacit knowledge often requires interaction; storing a document alone may not transfer judgment.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Apply the planned quality approach to project processes and work, evaluate whether those processes are capable, and improve them where needed.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Inspection at the end can find defects but cannot recover all wasted effort or prevent the same cause from recurring. Managing quality focuses on whether the methods used to create results are suitable and consistently applied. It turns quality planning into preventive and improvement activity during execution.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: The quality management plan and metrics establish the intended approach. Manage Quality uses execution evidence to assess and improve processes, and its findings can influence work practices, risk responses, or change requests; Control Quality separately measures specific results and deliverables. The activities recur as work and learning evolve.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Plan Quality Management defines the approach and measures. Manage Quality applies and improves the processes used to create results. Control Quality inspects results for conformance. Process capability and deliverable verification are related but different questions.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A customer-support transformation is producing inconsistent knowledge articles. The quality lead reviews the authoring and peer-review workflow, finds that approval roles are unclear, and introduces a clearer review method with coaching. Later sampling in Control Quality checks whether completed articles meet the defined criteria.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. A scenario about process improvement, assurance, or preventing recurring defects points toward Manage Quality.
  2. Inspection results can inform process improvement, but inspecting a deliverable remains Control Quality.
  3. Quality is built through the work process; it is not created solely by final testing.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Work directly with stakeholders to address needs and concerns, manage expectations, resolve issues, and support appropriate participation in project decisions and work.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Stakeholder support is not maintained through plans alone. Active engagement surfaces concerns early, builds shared understanding, and helps the project navigate competing expectations and change impacts. Avoiding difficult interactions allows resistance and misinformation to harden.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: The engagement plan and current stakeholder analysis guide day-to-day interaction. Outcomes, issues, and relationship changes feed communications, issue management, project decisions, and Monitor Stakeholder Engagement; approaches are adapted throughout the project.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Manage Stakeholder Engagement conducts the relationship work. Manage Communications handles project information flow, while Monitor Stakeholder Engagement evaluates whether the overall approach is achieving the needed involvement.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

During a factory automation project, operators fear job loss and supervisors worry about production disruption. The project manager facilitates demonstrations, listens to role concerns, involves operators in procedure design, and resolves an escalation about training time. Monitoring later checks whether participation and support improve.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Engagement focuses on relationships, expectations, participation, and issue resolution—not only message delivery.
  2. Address concerns at the appropriate level before defaulting to escalation.
  3. A changed stakeholder response may require revising the engagement strategy, not merely repeating the same communication.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Observe team performance, provide feedback, resolve issues, and coordinate changes needed to sustain effective project delivery.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Team conditions change as pressure, assignments, conflict, and performance evolve. Active management addresses those conditions before they damage work or relationships. It balances project needs with appropriate organizational authority rather than treating every problem as a training gap.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Performance observations, issue information, and team-development results inform management action. Feedback, conflict resolution, assignment changes, or escalations affect ongoing execution and may create new development or resource needs. The process continues throughout team participation.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Develop Team builds general capability and cohesion; Manage Team responds to current performance, feedback, conflict, and assignment conditions. Control Resources focuses primarily on physical-resource availability and use, not team leadership.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

Two engineering leads on a rail project are issuing incompatible interface decisions. The project manager meets with them, clarifies decision authority, resolves the immediate conflict, and adjusts the coordination routine. A broader interface workshop is then used as a team-development response.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. A specific conflict, feedback conversation, or performance correction points to Manage Team.
  2. Use appropriate authority and escalation paths; the project manager may not control every functional assignment.
  3. Do not confuse physical-resource variance with team performance management.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Evaluate overall project performance against the integrated plan so trends, forecasts, variances, and needed action are visible to decision-makers.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Local status reports do not automatically reveal whether the project as a whole remains viable or coordinated. Integrated monitoring turns performance information into a cross-project view and identifies where corrective, preventive, or replanning action may be needed. Passive observation would leave emerging problems unaddressed.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Execution and specialized control processes provide performance information, forecasts, and issues. This process synthesizes them, communicates the overall condition, and may produce change requests for formal review. It recurs throughout delivery and does not approve baseline changes by itself.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Monitor and Control Project Work assesses the project’s integrated health and recommends action. Perform Integrated Change Control evaluates and decides on change requests. Detecting a variance is not the same as approving its remedy.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A regional data-center migration is on budget, but vendor delays threaten the cutover window and increase operational risk. The project manager combines schedule, cost, risk, and readiness information into an overall forecast and recommends resequencing work. Any baseline change then goes through integrated change control.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Choose overall monitoring when the question combines information from several knowledge areas.
  2. Monitoring is active analysis and forecasting, not simply collecting status.
  3. A recommended corrective action becomes a change request when formal approval is required.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Evaluate whether project communication is meeting stakeholder information needs and adjust the approach when it is not.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: A communication can be delivered on time and still fail because it is misunderstood, ignored, inaccessible, or sent through the wrong channel. Monitoring looks beyond message counts to usefulness and effect. It keeps communication aligned with changing stakeholders and project conditions.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Actual communications, feedback, issue patterns, and stakeholder behavior are compared with the planned approach. Findings can change timing, format, channel, responsibility, or escalation and then influence Manage Communications. Evaluation recurs as information needs and project risk evolve.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Manage Communications creates and distributes project information. Monitor Communications determines whether that flow is effective. Monitor Stakeholder Engagement evaluates the broader relationship and involvement, of which communication is only one part.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A merger-integration project sends weekly updates, yet call-center supervisors continue acting on outdated procedures. Monitoring reveals that the email format is hard to use during shifts, so the team introduces supervisor huddles and a searchable change summary. Later feedback confirms fewer errors.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Evidence of delivery is not evidence of understanding or usefulness.
  2. Look for feedback, communication performance, or a need to change the communications approach.
  3. A stakeholder relationship problem may require engagement action beyond changing the message.

Hybrid treatmentAdaptive risk discovery and response are combined with program, contract, compliance, funding, or governance risk reporting. Why these badgesThe registered adaptive source explicitly describes these adaptive risk treatments and their use within hybrid governance.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Track identified and residual risks, detect emerging uncertainty, evaluate response effectiveness, and assess whether the risk-management approach remains useful.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Risk exposure changes as work proceeds, assumptions fail, responses are implemented, and new information appears. Monitoring keeps risk decisions connected to current reality and prevents closed or outdated entries from dominating attention. It also tests whether the project’s risk practices are working.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Execution evidence, risk-owner updates, response results, issues, and project forecasts provide the monitoring basis. Findings may identify new risks, close obsolete ones, trigger planned responses, revise priorities, or create change requests and feed another cycle of analysis and planning.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Monitor Risks evaluates exposure and response performance across the project. Implement Risk Responses carries out planned actions. Monitoring can trigger or adjust work, but it is not passive observation or a substitute for implementation.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

During a cloud-service transition, the team reviews migration errors, supplier capacity, security findings, and response actions. A previously minor identity risk is escalating while a data-volume risk has retired. The team reprioritizes exposure, activates an agreed test response, and identifies a new vendor-concentration risk.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Monitoring includes new-risk identification, trigger review, response evaluation, and overall process effectiveness.
  2. An issue that has occurred may require immediate management while its effects also inform risk monitoring.
  3. Risk status is dynamic; do not preserve an outdated ranking merely because it was approved during planning.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Evaluate stakeholder relationships and involvement, detect changes in support or influence, and adjust engagement strategies when needed.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: A strategy that worked early may fail after a decision, organizational change, or visible project impact. Monitoring compares actual involvement with what the project needs and identifies relationship risks before they block progress. It treats engagement as an adaptive management concern.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Feedback, participation patterns, issues, decisions, and stakeholder behavior provide evidence. Findings update stakeholder analysis and engagement approaches and influence Manage Stakeholder Engagement and communications; evaluation continues as the project and its environment change.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Monitor Stakeholder Engagement assesses relationship effectiveness and needed adjustment. Manage Stakeholder Engagement performs the interactions, while Monitor Communications evaluates whether information needs are being met.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

On a neighborhood flood-control project, public meeting attendance is stable but comments show that renters believe only property owners influence decisions. The team recognizes an engagement gap, adds tenant outreach through local organizations, and measures whether participation becomes more representative.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Attendance or message delivery alone does not prove effective engagement.
  2. Look for comparison between current and needed involvement followed by a strategy adjustment.
  3. Stakeholder influence and attitude can change suddenly after a project decision or external event.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Evaluate change requests in an integrated context, decide their disposition through the authorized governance process, and coordinate approved changes.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: A change that helps one objective can damage another by altering scope, schedule, cost, quality, risk, or stakeholder commitments. Integrated review makes those tradeoffs visible before authorization. Without it, local decisions can quietly invalidate baselines and create incompatible promises.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Change requests may arise from execution, monitoring, risk responses, quality findings, or stakeholder needs. Their impacts are assessed against the project management plan and other current information; approved changes are then incorporated and implemented through the appropriate work. The process operates whenever controlled change is needed, not only at a scheduled gate.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Perform Integrated Change Control approves, rejects, defers, or otherwise disposes of requests. Direct and Manage Project Work implements what has been approved. A team should not begin baseline-changing work merely because a request has been submitted.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A medical-device project proposes replacing a component after a supplier warning. The change authority reviews regulatory, quality, schedule, cost, inventory, and validation impacts before approving the replacement. Planning records are updated, and the delivery team then implements the authorized design change.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Follow the change request to the authorized decision before selecting implementation activity.
  2. Assess cross-project effects; an isolated technical benefit does not establish overall approval.
  3. Configuration and baseline updates follow the decision according to the project’s governance approach.

docs.title: Delivery approach applicability
docs.text:
→Predictive↻Adaptive⇄Hybrid Predictive treatmentUses the formally named risk process and documented analysis, response, ownership, and monitoring practices. Adaptive equivalent or treatmentRisk is addressed through short feedback loops, prioritization, experiments, spikes, incremental delivery, frequent review, and retrospective improvement. Hybrid treatmentAdaptive risk discovery and response are combined with program, contract, compliance, funding, or governance risk reporting. Why these badgesThe registered adaptive source explicitly describes these adaptive risk treatments and their use within hybrid governance.

Source-limited crosswalk: Predictive classification is supported by the canonical process catalog. Cross-approach treatments are an Atlas synthesis of the registered 2026 course snapshot and are not a PMI process-to-agile-framework crosswalk.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Prioritize identified risks using relative probability, impact, urgency, and other agreed characteristics so attention goes where it matters most.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Treating every risk as equally important overwhelms the team and wastes response effort. Qualitative analysis applies a consistent, context-aware comparison and exposes where data quality or stakeholder perception may distort priorities. It supports efficient escalation and deeper analysis.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: The risk register and planned scales provide the starting point. Prioritized risks move to response planning, while selected high-impact or complex uncertainties may receive quantitative analysis; the priorities are revisited as exposure changes. The result is relative ranking, not a numerical forecast of overall project outcomes.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Qualitative analysis ranks individual risks using agreed relative criteria. Quantitative analysis models numerical effects on objectives and combined uncertainty when useful. High priority does not automatically mean a risk requires quantitative modeling.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A university system ranks migration risks using agreed probability, service impact, urgency, and detectability criteria. Loss of historical records and identity-integration failure receive immediate attention, while a minor reporting-format risk is placed on a watch list. One schedule-sensitive risk is selected for numerical analysis.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Look for prioritization, relative scales, urgency, or categorization rather than numerical outcome distributions.
  2. Bias and poor data quality can affect rankings, so facilitation and agreed definitions matter.
  3. The next step for a prioritized risk may be response planning, further analysis, or monitoring depending on context.

docs.title: Delivery approach applicability
docs.text:
→Predictive Predictive treatmentPerformed as the formally named process within the Process Group model, with the level of definition and control tailored to the project. Adaptive equivalent or treatmentIts management purpose may still be relevant, but the registered evidence does not support presenting the formally named process as an adaptive practice. Hybrid treatmentA hybrid project may use the process for governed or fixed elements, but use is context-specific and is not asserted as common here. Why these badgesThe canonical catalog supports the named predictive process; current sources do not support a stronger cross-approach classification.

Source-limited crosswalk: Predictive classification is supported by the canonical process catalog. Cross-approach treatments are an Atlas synthesis of the registered 2026 course snapshot and are not a PMI process-to-agile-framework crosswalk.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Numerically evaluate the combined effect of uncertainty on project objectives and estimate the range or likelihood of important outcomes when such analysis is warranted.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Relative rankings cannot answer questions such as how likely a target is or how much aggregate uncertainty surrounds a cost or date. Quantitative analysis combines selected risk and model uncertainty to support high-stakes decisions. It requires suitable data and is not automatically valuable on every project.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Prioritized risks, schedule or cost models, assumptions, and credible data provide the basis. Results inform response planning, contingency decisions, target confidence, and later monitoring; models are updated when exposure or data changes. The analysis supplements judgment rather than replacing it.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Perform Qualitative Risk Analysis prioritizes risks with relative criteria. Perform Quantitative Risk Analysis uses numerical modeling to examine combined effects on objectives. Quantitative analysis is performed when decision value and data justify it, not simply because a risk is important.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

An offshore maintenance shutdown has tightly coupled tasks and costly delay exposure. The team models uncertain repair durations, weather windows, and specialist availability to estimate the probability of reopening by the target date. The results support added contingency and a backup specialist agreement.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Choose quantitative analysis when the scenario asks about numerical confidence, aggregate exposure, or outcome ranges.
  2. A model is only as useful as its assumptions and data; false precision is not stronger risk management.
  3. Not every project or prioritized risk requires quantitative analysis.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Define how project information will be created, formatted, distributed, stored, retrieved, protected, and monitored for different stakeholder needs.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Sending more information does not guarantee understanding or timely decisions. Communications planning matches content, channel, timing, responsibility, and accessibility to the people who need the information. Poor planning creates overload for some stakeholders and dangerous information gaps for others.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Stakeholder analysis, project context, information sensitivity, and delivery practices shape the communications approach. The plan guides Manage Communications and provides expectations later evaluated by Monitor Communications; it evolves when stakeholder needs, technology, or project conditions change.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Plan Communications Management designs the approach. Manage Communications creates and distributes information using that approach, while Monitor Communications evaluates whether the approach and actual communications are meeting stakeholder needs.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A regulatory remediation project maps executives to concise risk decisions, site teams to daily action updates, regulators to controlled submissions, and technical specialists to detailed evidence repositories. It assigns owners, timing, security, and escalation channels. Delivery and monitoring then use those expectations.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. The best channel depends on the audience, urgency, complexity, sensitivity, and need for feedback.
  2. A communications plan is not merely a meeting calendar or distribution list.
  3. If stakeholders are not receiving useful information, monitoring should evaluate effectiveness before blindly increasing volume.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Define how project costs will be estimated, aggregated, funded, reported, and controlled.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Cost figures are difficult to compare when teams use different units, assumptions, reporting periods, or control rules. This process establishes a coherent financial-management approach before detailed estimates and budgets are produced. The approach should reflect the project’s size, uncertainty, contracts, and governance needs.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: The charter, integrated planning context, schedule approach, and organizational financial practices shape the method. It guides Estimate Costs, Determine Budget, and Control Costs and may be refined if funding or delivery conditions change. It defines how cost work will be performed rather than calculating the costs.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Plan Cost Management sets the cost-management method. Estimate Costs develops estimates for project work, Determine Budget aggregates them into an authorized baseline and funding view, and Control Costs evaluates actual performance.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A nonprofit preparing a multi-country training program agrees on currencies, estimating precision, contingency treatment, reporting cycles, approval thresholds, and how donor restrictions will be tracked. Teams then prepare comparable estimates and a fundable budget.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Questions about cost rules and approach precede the creation of estimates or a budget.
  2. Tailor precision and control effort to the decision need; more decimal places do not create certainty.
  3. Cost planning should align with schedule, procurement, and risk planning rather than operate independently.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Decide what project needs should be obtained externally and define how solicitation, selection, contracting, oversight, and closure will be handled.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: External sourcing transfers some work but introduces commercial, legal, schedule, quality, and relationship obligations. Procurement planning makes the make-or-buy reasoning and acquisition approach explicit before the project commits to a seller. Weak planning produces unclear requirements and contracts that cannot be managed effectively.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Scope, schedule, cost, resource, risk, and organizational procurement rules inform the decision. The resulting approach guides Conduct Procurements and later Control Procurements and may change when market conditions or project needs change. Planning does not select the seller or create the final agreement.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Plan Procurement Management decides what and how to buy. Conduct Procurements evaluates seller responses and establishes an agreement, while Control Procurements manages performance and the contractual relationship.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A utility decides to obtain specialized drone inspection externally because it lacks certified pilots and equipment. The team defines the service boundary, evaluation approach, safety and data requirements, commercial responsibilities, and oversight method. Procurement staff then solicit and evaluate sellers.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. A make-or-buy or procurement-strategy question belongs in planning before seller selection.
  2. Clear scope and acceptance expectations support both fair selection and later contract control.
  3. Procurement decisions can alter risk, schedule, cost, and stakeholder commitments, so they are not isolated purchasing actions.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Plan Quality Management establishes the quality approach for the project before significant work begins. It defines how quality will be planned, measured, and evaluated so that later processes can apply consistent standards.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Quality planning is needed because work cannot be judged effectively without agreed standards. If the project does not define what acceptable performance looks like, later inspection and verification activities will lack a clear basis.

docs.title: Position in the Project
docs.text:
This process occurs when the project has enough information about scope and requirements to define quality expectations. It is typically performed during planning, after requirements and scope information are available and before work is executed at scale.

Quality planning depends on requirements and scope information because those sources establish what the result must do and what acceptance means. The planning processes may overlap and iterate as that information develops.

Within Project Quality Management, this is process 1 of 3. Within the broader Quality Management relationship sequence—which also shows inputs, artifacts, and the contextual Validate Scope process—it is step 2 of 8.

docs.title: How the Quality Sequence Unfolds
docs.text:
1. Planning

    Requirements and acceptance expectations are documented. Requirements Documentation, the Requirements Traceability Matrix, and the scope baseline provide the basis for meaningful quality decisions.

  2. Planning

    Plan Quality Management is performed. The process translates requirements and acceptance expectations into a usable quality approach.

  3. Planning

    The Quality Management Plan and Quality Metrics are created. The plan defines how quality will be managed; the metrics define measurable criteria for later evaluation.

  4. Executing

    Manage Quality applies and improves the planned quality processes. The team uses the Quality Management Plan and Quality Metrics while carrying out the work.

  5. Monitoring and Controlling

    Control Quality inspects and measures deliverables. Inspection and test results are recorded as Quality-Control Measurements.

  6. Monitoring and Controlling

    Verified Deliverables have passed inspection. Control Quality confirms that the deliverables meet the specified requirements.

  7. Monitoring and Controlling

    Validate Scope obtains formal acceptance. The authorized stakeholder reviews the Verified Deliverables and makes the acceptance decision.

  8. Monitoring and Controlling

    Accepted Deliverables are confirmed. Their status records the formal acceptance decision and makes them ready for transition or further project use.

The sequence expresses logical dependency rather than a fixed, one-time chronology. Planning and delivery activities may overlap or iterate as the project changes.

docs.title: Primary Inputs
docs.text:
Requirements Documentation

Defines the capabilities and conditions that quality planning must translate into measurable expectations.

Requirements Traceability Matrix

Connects requirements to their sources and planned verification, reducing the risk that a requirement lacks a quality check.

Scope Baseline

Provides the approved scope, deliverable descriptions, and work boundaries that the quality approach must support.

Stakeholder Register

Identifies people whose expectations, authority, or expertise influence quality and acceptance decisions.

Risk Register

Identifies uncertainties that may require preventive controls, additional review, or more stringent thresholds.

Assumption Log

Surfaces assumptions and constraints that affect how quality can be achieved or measured.

docs.title: Secondary Inputs
docs.text:
1. The Project Charter supplies high-level objectives, success criteria, and authority.
  2. The Project Scope Statement adds detailed deliverable and acceptance information as it becomes available.
  3. Relevant components of the Project Management Plan align the quality approach with requirements, risks, and scope.
  4. The Lessons Learned Register provides prior experience with methods, thresholds, defects, and reviews.
  5. Enterprise Environmental Factors and Organizational Process Assets may provide regulations, standards, policies, templates, and historical information.

docs.title: Tools & Techniques
docs.text:
1. Cost-benefit analysis
  2. Benchmarking
  3. Design of experiments
  4. Statistical sampling
  5. Quality management and control tools
  6. Expert judgment

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text: New artifacts Existing records

docs.title: Created by this process
docs.text:
Quality Management Plan

Describes how quality will be managed and controlled, including roles, methods, review activity, and reporting expectations.

Quality Metrics

Defines the specific measurements, methods, and acceptable values used to evaluate project and product quality.

docs.title: May be updated
docs.text:
Quality planning can change existing commitments or add information to records that already exist. It does not create these artifacts. The Project Management Plan is updated when a quality decision affects an existing plan component.

  1. Lessons Learned Register
  2. Requirements Traceability Matrix
  3. Risk Register
  4. Stakeholder Register

These four registers are Project Documents; the panel separates them from the governing Project Management Plan.

docs.title: Used Next By
docs.text:
1. Manage Quality applies the planned quality approach to project processes and work.
  2. Control Quality compares actual results with the plan and metrics.
  3. Direct and Manage Project Work uses the quality approach while creating deliverables.
  4. Validate Scope depends indirectly on the planning outputs because verified deliverables reach acceptance only after Control Quality applies the defined criteria.

docs.title: How the Outputs Evolve
docs.text: The Quality Management Plan and Quality Metrics are created during planning, applied during execution and quality activity, and retained as the basis for later measurement and verification. They may be updated when approved changes alter scope, requirements, risks, or delivery assumptions. At closure, the current versions and associated quality records become part of the project archive.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Locate the scenario in the sequence before selecting a process. A question about defining the method or measurable criteria points to planning; a question about applying or improving that method points to Manage Quality.
  2. Use the artifact’s current state to determine what happens next. An inspected result belongs in Control Quality; a verified deliverable is ready for the formal acceptance decision in Validate Scope.
  3. Separate conformance evidence from stakeholder authority. Passing a technical check does not itself mean the deliverable has been accepted.
  4. Watch the verb in a change scenario. Creating a quality approach produces new planning artifacts; reflecting an approved quality decision in an existing record is an update.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE Website account registration

A product team must ensure that a new account can be created reliably under expected traffic.

  1. RequirementThe registration form must return a confirmation within two seconds for at least 95 percent of valid submissions.
  2. Quality metric95th-percentile response time is no more than 2.0 seconds under the defined test load.
  3. Inspection resultControl Quality records a 95th-percentile response time of 1.7 seconds.
  4. VerificationThe tested form meets the specified threshold and becomes part of a verified deliverable.
  5. Formal acceptanceDuring Validate Scope, the authorized product owner reviews the verified result and accepts the deliverable.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Define how team and physical resources will be estimated, acquired, developed, managed, controlled, and released.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Resource decisions shape both the feasibility of the work and the conditions under which people perform it. A deliberate approach clarifies roles, responsibilities, acquisition choices, team practices, and physical-resource governance before shortages or conflicts become urgent. The approach should distinguish people-management needs from control of equipment, materials, and facilities.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Scope, schedule, cost, quality, and organizational context inform the resource approach. It guides Estimate Activity Resources, Acquire Resources, Develop Team, Manage Team, and Control Resources and is refined as assignments or delivery conditions change. Planning the approach does not itself secure a named person or piece of equipment.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Plan Resource Management defines the approach and responsibilities. Estimate Activity Resources determines what activities need, Acquire Resources obtains those resources, and the later development, management, and control processes address different aspects of their use.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A hospital network plans a new telehealth service. The team defines clinical and technical roles, staffing authority, equipment ownership, onboarding expectations, escalation paths, and how loaned devices will be tracked and released. Those decisions guide detailed estimates and later acquisition.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Resource Management covers both team resources and physical resources, but not every downstream process treats them identically.
  2. A method or responsibility question belongs in planning; a quantity question belongs in Estimate Activity Resources.
  3. Team development and team performance management are not substitutes for obtaining the needed people.

docs.title: Delivery approach applicability
docs.text:
→Predictive↻Adaptive⇄Hybrid Predictive treatmentUses the formally named risk process and documented analysis, response, ownership, and monitoring practices. Adaptive equivalent or treatmentRisk is addressed through short feedback loops, prioritization, experiments, spikes, incremental delivery, frequent review, and retrospective improvement. Hybrid treatmentAdaptive risk discovery and response are combined with program, contract, compliance, funding, or governance risk reporting. Why these badgesThe registered adaptive source explicitly describes these adaptive risk treatments and their use within hybrid governance.

Source-limited crosswalk: Predictive classification is supported by the canonical process catalog. Cross-approach treatments are an Atlas synthesis of the registered 2026 course snapshot and are not a PMI process-to-agile-framework crosswalk.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Define how risk management will be conducted, governed, resourced, communicated, and integrated with the rest of the project.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Risk activity becomes inconsistent when participants use different scales, categories, ownership expectations, or review routines. This process establishes a proportionate approach before detailed identification and analysis. The needed rigor depends on uncertainty, stakes, and organizational context.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: The charter, stakeholder environment, delivery approach, and organizational practices shape the risk-management method. It guides identification, qualitative and quantitative analysis where appropriate, response planning, implementation, and monitoring and can be refined when project exposure changes.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Plan Risk Management designs the risk process. Identify Risks discovers specific uncertainties, and the analysis processes evaluate their relative or numerical significance. Planning the method is not listing the risks.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A coastal infrastructure program agrees on risk categories, probability and impact scales, ownership, escalation authority, review cadence, and when numerical analysis is justified. That common approach lets engineering, environmental, community, and funding teams analyze uncertainty consistently.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. If the question is about scales, roles, cadence, or methodology, risk planning comes before identifying individual events.
  2. Risk management should be proportionate; quantitative analysis is not mandatory for every project or every risk.
  3. The risk approach must connect with schedule, cost, procurement, and stakeholder decisions.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Select proportionate actions for prioritized threats and opportunities, assign ownership, and integrate the chosen responses with project work.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Analysis alone does not change exposure. Response planning turns risk understanding into feasible, owned action while checking that a response does not create an unacceptable secondary risk or conflict with project objectives. Vague intentions without ownership rarely affect execution.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Prioritized risks and any quantitative insight inform strategy and action selection. Agreed responses influence scope, schedule, cost, procurement, communications, or resource plans and are later carried out through Implement Risk Responses; residual and new risks continue into monitoring.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Plan Risk Responses chooses and prepares the actions. Implement Risk Responses ensures those agreed actions are performed. Monitor Risks evaluates exposure and response effectiveness afterward.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A product launch faces a threat that certification testing may overrun and an opportunity to enter a partner channel early. The team assigns an owner, books an alternate test slot, and prepares evidence earlier for the threat; it also defines a limited partner pilot for the opportunity. Those actions are added to the delivery plan.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. A response should be owned, feasible, timely, and proportionate to the risk.
  2. Planning a response does not mean it has been implemented.
  3. Consider residual and secondary risks rather than assuming the chosen action removes all uncertainty.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Define how the project schedule will be developed, maintained, reported, and controlled at a level appropriate to the work.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Activity dates are unreliable when teams use inconsistent calendars, units, update rules, or control thresholds. Schedule planning establishes the method and governance before the detailed model is built. It prevents later arguments about how progress and forecast changes should be represented.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: The integrated planning context, delivery approach, and organizational practices shape the schedule-management method. That method guides activity definition, sequencing, duration estimation, schedule development, and schedule control. It may be tailored as uncertainty, release structure, or reporting needs evolve.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Plan Schedule Management defines the scheduling approach. Develop Schedule applies activity, dependency, duration, resource, and constraint information to produce and analyze the schedule model.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

An event-production team agrees on milestone definitions, working calendars, update frequency, progress measurement, and how rehearsal changes will be controlled before building the detailed festival schedule. Producers then use the common rules when integrating venue, performer, vendor, and permit activities.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. A question about scheduling rules or methodology belongs here; a question about calculated dates belongs in Develop Schedule.
  2. The schedule-management approach should fit the delivery environment rather than impose one universal level of detail.
  3. Planning how the schedule will be controlled precedes measuring an actual schedule variance.

docs.text: Define how scope and requirements will be developed, validated, and controlled so the project has a consistent way to make boundary decisions.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Teams cannot manage scope consistently if they have not agreed how requirements will be gathered, decomposition will occur, acceptance will be obtained, and changes will be handled. This planning process establishes that approach before detailed scope work expands. The needed formality should match project complexity and governance.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: The charter and integrated planning context shape the scope-management approach. That approach guides Collect Requirements, Define Scope, Create WBS, Validate Scope, and Control Scope, and it may be refined when the project’s delivery model or uncertainty changes. It does not itself discover the requirements or define the detailed scope.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Plan Scope Management decides how scope work will be performed. Collect Requirements discovers stakeholder needs, and Define Scope turns selected needs and constraints into a detailed project and product boundary.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

An association is planning a national conference. Before interviewing speakers and attendees, the team agrees how needs will be documented, how the event scope will be decomposed, who can accept major deliverables, and how proposed scope changes will be evaluated. Those rules keep later content and venue decisions consistent.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. A question about the method for managing scope points here; a question about actual needs points to Collect Requirements.
  2. Tailoring the scope approach is expected—the same level of documentation is not required for every project.
  3. Validation and control are anticipated during planning even though they occur repeatedly later.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Choose tailored approaches for involving stakeholders based on their needs, expectations, influence, impact, and current relationship with the project.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Knowing who stakeholders are does not determine how to work with them. Engagement planning anticipates support, resistance, decision needs, cultural context, and the effort required to maintain productive involvement. A single communication approach can alienate some groups while failing to reach others.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Stakeholder identification and current project plans provide the analytical basis. The chosen strategies guide Manage Stakeholder Engagement and are evaluated and adjusted through Monitor Stakeholder Engagement; they evolve as influence, attitude, or project impact changes.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Identify Stakeholders determines who matters and analyzes initial characteristics. Plan Stakeholder Engagement selects the engagement approach, while Manage Stakeholder Engagement performs the interactions. Communications planning supports but does not replace engagement planning.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A university introduces a new advising model. The project plans co-design workshops with advisers, decision briefings with deans, accessibility reviews with student groups, and targeted support for departments likely to resist role changes. Those strategies guide ongoing engagement rather than simply distributing announcements.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Engagement is tailored to influence, impact, expectations, and current versus desired involvement.
  2. A stakeholder’s attitude can change, so the plan is not a one-time classification exercise.
  3. Sending information may support engagement but does not by itself resolve expectations or build commitment.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Determine and document the logical relationships among schedule activities so the project can model a feasible order of work.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: A complete activity list still cannot show when work can occur. Dependencies reveal what must precede, follow, or overlap other work and expose the consequences of a delay. Weak sequencing creates impossible dates and hides coordination constraints.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Defined activities and known constraints provide the starting point. The resulting network relationships combine with duration and resource information during Develop Schedule; they are revisited when execution, approved changes, or new constraints alter the logic. Sequencing establishes order, not calendar dates by itself.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Sequence Activities establishes dependency logic. Develop Schedule analyzes that logic together with durations, resources, calendars, and constraints to determine planned dates.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A theater renovation team maps that structural inspection must precede wall closure, electrical rough-in can overlap with some plumbing work, and seating installation must follow floor finishing. When a permit date shifts, the dependency model shows which rehearsals and commissioning activities are affected.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Dependencies answer 'in what logical order?' rather than 'how long?' or 'on what date?'
  2. A network can include overlap where justified; sequencing does not require every activity to be strictly finish-to-start.
  3. Use the relationship logic to reason about downstream effects of a delayed activity.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Obtain formal acceptance of completed deliverables from the authorized customer, sponsor, or other accepting stakeholder.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Technical completion does not establish that the authorized stakeholder agrees the result satisfies the accepted need. Formal validation makes the acceptance decision explicit and provides a basis for transition, payment, closure, or corrective action. Without it, teams may mistake internal confidence for customer acceptance.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Control Quality supplies deliverables that have been verified against defined quality requirements. Validate Scope presents those results for formal review and records acceptance or the need for further action; it can occur repeatedly as deliverables are completed. Accepted deliverables support phase or project closure.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Control Quality determines whether a deliverable conforms to specified quality requirements and produces verified deliverables. Validate Scope obtains formal acceptance from the authorized stakeholder. Verified does not automatically mean accepted.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A contractor completes a renovated school science lab. Inspection confirms that fixtures, ventilation, and safety systems meet the specified criteria, producing a verified deliverable. The school authority then reviews the completed lab, resolves an acceptance comment, and formally accepts it for use.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Follow the state of the deliverable: checked for conformance means Control Quality; presented for formal acceptance means Validate Scope.
  2. Acceptance authority belongs to the designated stakeholder, not simply the project team.
  3. Validation may happen for individual deliverables before the entire project is ready to close.
